#5602. Chip and Joanna Gaines Are Talking About Having Another Baby: ‘He Is Telling Everyone I’m Pregnant’

Chip and Joanna Gaines are talking about expanding their family.

During a Nov. 5 appearance on Kylie Kelce’s podcast, “Not Gonna Lie,” Joanna revealed that her husband of 23 years has come down with a case of baby fever.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” the HGTV star said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

“He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” she continued.

“He told our grown kids, ‘Mom is pregnant.’ My daughter said, ‘I’m not coming home if this is true,’” Joanna, 48, explained, adding that Chip, 51, is “like, trying to speak it out into the universe,”

According to the mom of five, at a recent public speaking appearance the couple had “in front of 2,000” people, Chip told the crowd, “If anyone has any connection to TMZ, will you tell them that my wife is [pregnant]?”

“So that whole audience thinks I’m pregnant. I don’t know what’s happening,” said the “Fixer Upper” personality. “But I’m not.”

Joanna went on to try to convince Kylie to expand her family, too, adding that she’d “have more babies” if she “could.”

She told the podcast host that “five is a good number… five is so special,” and even offered to design a nursery for a potential addition to the Kelce family.

“I’m just saying, Kylie, bust it out. Five,” she urged. “It’s going to be your little boy, and it’s going to rock your world because it’s totally different than girls. And it’s another spot in your heart. And if it’s a girl, great because five girls is a party house.”

Joanna reflected on her own motherhood experience, adding that she and Chip “weren’t planning anything” when they had their first four children—Drake, 21, Ella, 20, Duke, 18, and Emmy, who will soon be 17.

The couple welcomed their fifth child, 8-year-old Crew, in June 2018.

“At one point, I had three in diapers still,” she said. “I just feel like it was so chaotic and fun and I loved it.”

Joanna told Kylie that she’s particularly enjoying the stage of life she’s in, as her eldest children navigate early adulthood.

In September, during an appearance on “Joy 101 with Hoda Kotb,” Joanna opened up about the “mom guilt” she’s experienced while balancing her professional life as she raises five children.

She explained that although she was a “stay-at-home mom” for a time, she feared she had missed out on key moments with her children as her business ramped up.

The feelings came to a head as she recently drove her daughter, Ella, to the airport to go to college.

“I remember crying a little bit and thinking, ‘OK, this is the moment I can just say I’m sorry for anywhere I wasn’t present,’” she recalled. “For months, what I was grieving was, ‘I wasn’t home the whole time.’”

Joanna apologized to her daughter for her time spent away from the home, and was shocked when Ella “kind of got mad” in response.

“She got upset and said, ‘Mom, are you serious? All you’ve taught me is I can do everything and anything,’” Joanna revealed.

Regardless of whether the Gainses decide to expand their family, the Waco, TX, couple certainly has their hands full.

Chip and Joanna are set to tackle their most involved renovation yet in the brand-new series, “Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion.”

The six-episode series will follow the couple’s journey as they embark on a three-month project to transform a 15,000-square-foot estate Chip bought in their hometown three years ago.

In a classic twist of reality TV luck, the Gaineses soon discover that the property needs much more work than they had originally anticipated.

“Chip has always been a dreamer and risk taker, but even for him, buying a mansion was a bold move,” Joanna remarked in a statement shared with Realtor.com®.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. #5601. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5600. Democrats Will Focus on Affordability in 2027, Party Leaders Say

Democrats rode affordability anxieties to big wins in the midterm elections. But they must deliver on lowering costs if they want to sustain their political power, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Thursday.

Speaking at a Washington, DC, forum hosted by Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank, Schumer reflected on the significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats were able to flip dozens of seats and gain control of both the House and Senate for the upcoming Congress.

Democrats spent the year attacking President Donald Trump on "costs, chaos, and corruption," as Schumer put it. But although many people voted for Democrats out of frustration with the Trump administration, that doesn't mean they're enthusiastic about the Democratic Party, he conceded.

"We highlighted how Trump's chaos agenda was causing Americans pain at the grocery store, at the gas pump," Schumer said. "Every month in the spring, we focused on the costs of the American people and what we were going to do about it."

Vice President JD Vance has also said that the conflict in Iran and subsequent inflation surge cost Republicans the election. Schumer said Democrats have to bring down costs. Ending the Iran conflict and stopping the tariffs policies that have driven up costs in the country are two ways to do that.

Although Democrats made major gains, they still won't have enough votes to override a Trump veto. And Democratic leadership will have to find common ground with the party's left flank after a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates won elections on Tuesday, a fact Schumer acknowledged without mentioning the group by name.

"Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree," Schumer said. "Intra-party debate isn't a sign of weakness."

Democrats who won state and local races have promised affordability-minded reforms and emphasized housing production. That's crucial in expensive areas such as California and Washington DC.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said at the CAP event that medical and student debt are also issues Democrats should tackle at the federal level. These debts significantly delay homeownership. But he said both oversight and affordability should be Congress' main focus next year.

"You can walk and chew gum, we have to deal with affordability, that has to be the principal thing," Pritzer said. "But we have to have oversight committees, just like the Republicans did."

On Wednesday, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out an agenda. But Democrats would focus on "affordability and accountability" with their new majority, he said.

Democrats after the election threw out a host of ideas for items to pursue in 2027 and 2028. Many of them focused on both affordability and guardrails for artificial intelligence and data centers.

"Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence," Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) posted to X on Wednesday.

The Nasdaq plunged 5% the next day, led by a sharp decline in tech stocks.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who caucuses with the Democrats, called for a national 5% wealth tax in a video message Thursday morning. Such a tax, as is being considered in California, could fund 7 million units of affordable housing, Sanders said.

Realtor.com® economists quantified just how bad the affordability situation is for Americans.

In January, a $2,000 monthly mortgage payment supported a home price $28,500 higher than a year earlier. By October 2026, that same payment supported a home price $33,600 lower. The surge in interest rates, from 6.05% in February to 7.33% in October, was to blame for the $62,100 swing.

“Mortgage rates are not abstract to a family trying to buy a home,” says Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “They show up as the home they can no longer afford."

"The year-over-year comparison is a vivid measure of why housing affordability lands as a pocketbook issue for voters," Hale continues. "The conflict’s inflationary impact is one source of uncertainty, but households feel the consequences in their monthly budgets and in the homes they have to take off their list.”

In a post, National Association of Homebuilders Chief Advocacy Officer Ken Wingert urged the next Congress to craft more housing bills like the comprehensive 21st Century Road to Housing Act that passed this summer.

Lawmakers have suggested they have their own sets of ideas for new housing measures to pursue. Cities and localities, they have said, must also step up to implement new laws.

Those rules must assuage builders whose confidence has been shattered by high costs of building materials and high mortgage rates chasing homebuyers out of the market. The National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell to a 14-year low last month.

"With a national housing shortfall of roughly 1.2 million households, more must be done to let builders build—and voters agree," Wingert said. "Throughout the campaign, voters consistently cited housing availability and affordability as key factors in their decisions."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5599. Aina’s smart AI ring promises a new way to interact with AI agents that anticipate user’s needs

Artificial intelligence has come a long way in a very short space of time, writing emails, answering questions, generating code, images, video and more besides. But as breathtaking as these advances are, using AI is still a hassle. People have to dig out their smartphone and find the right app, then enter a prompt before anything gets done.

Seeking to eliminate this friction is a startup called Aina Computers Inc., which has just emerged from 15 months in “stealth mode” to launch its flagship product: an AI-native smart ring equipped with an OLED display that’s purpose-built to control autonomous AI agents.

Aina founder Apoorv Shankar told SiliconANGLE that the development of hardware interfaces has not kept pace with the advances in AI. For people to access intelligence, they need to go fumbling through smartphone applications or switch on a laptop.

Even the most basic tasks, like ordering an Uber, require someone to open an app, enter their destination and click to confirm. To join a virtual meeting, the user still has to dig through their emails to find the right link. In Shankar’s view, AI is trapped behind a software layer and that means it cannot proactively serve people when they need it.

Aina’s Ring is meant to free AI from these binds and make it as simple to access as uttering a command. The Ring is made from titanium and comes equipped with a colorful OLED display, a microphone and a speaker, and an 18-hour battery. There’s also a mechanical “shifter” that can track thumb gestures in four directions.. “We started building Aina with a thesis that AI would evolve from following instructions to anticipating what we need,” Shankar explained.

The device is powered by Aina’s Context Aware Operating System software, which is designed to learn the Ring wearer’s behavior over time in order to anticipate their needs. It can connect to the user’s devices, such as their smartphone and computer, and also any AI agents they use. Once it’s up and running, it tries to anticipate what users will need at any given moment and surface the information they need on the Ring’s display before they even ask for it.

“With proactive agents, this shift has already begun,” Shankar said. “Agents like Muse, Instinct and Dots will soon run hundreds of our daily tasks, yet we still have to instruct them by text or voice. But soon, they’ll learn our patterns, build on our context and turn proactive for almost every interaction, waiting only for our approval.”

Shankar founded Aina last year. The startup was originally a human-computer interaction research lab. Its 40-person team experimented with dozens of different hardware concepts, including an adaptive three-key Mac keypad called Dune, before ultimately settling on the Ring as the ultimate interface for AI agents.

Aina’s $399 Ring is available for pre-order now and will ship to customers in January. That’s the date at which people’s relationship with AI is set to fundamentally change, Shankar believes. When someone wears Aina’s Ring, the way they interact with their AI agents will generally become a matter of simply saying yes or no, for they will quickly learn to anticipate what their users need, at the moment they need it, he said.

Users can interact with the Ring in three ways. The microphone is there to support voice interactions. The user simply presses and holds the button in the center to call up an agent and instruct it to do something, or else they can just use it to record some quick notes. It will also be able to relay phone calls, enabling people to converse by just holding their hand close to their ear.

The Ring also supports cues that are powered by the context-aware operating system. As it learns to anticipate user’s needs, it will be able to proactively order an Uber ride based on the time of day, their location and their schedule. All the user has to do is click or say “yes” to confirm and the Ring will book the ride. Alternatively, if someone is late for an appointment, the Ring will proactively draft a message to let the person they’re meeting know when they’ll arrive.

Shankar said the Ring can also be used as a remote control, so if someone is watching TV they’ll be able to tell it to pause or rewind the show they’re watching. It can adjust microphones and cameras during video calls, skip to the next track when someone’s listening to music on their iPod and so on.

“Every major shift in computing has come from software and hardware built together,” Shankar said. “The mouse and GUI brought us personal computing. The touchscreen and the app gave us mobile computing. Now with Aina we enter a new era, with personalized computing right at your fingertips.”

#5598. Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

#5596. Oracle’s multicloud approach: Put the database wherever AI pipelines already run

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are learning that real-time data pipelines matter as much as the models. An agent working from a stale subset of corporate records delivers far less than one wired into live, mission-critical data.

That shift is changing how companies decide where their databases run. Oracle Corp. has pushed its database modernization strategy into other clouds, and customers are moving databases next to the applications and AI pipelines they are building, according to Nathan Thomas (pictured), senior vice president of product management for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle.

“Customers are defining their AI pipelines, I think from an enterprise business perspective, with an eye towards trust, with an eye towards security,” Thomas said. “They are really looking at, ‘How do I get the mission-critical data into those pipelines?'”

Thomas spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how real-time data pipelines help improve agentic AI performance. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle offers its database on its own cloud, on-premises through Cloud@Customer and inside Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Azure and Google LLC’s Google Cloud. Customers rarely ask which cloud to pick, since existing relationships and the location of their applications usually settle the question, Thomas explained.

“They’re usually saying, ‘Hey, I’ve already got a relationship. Let’s put the database where my apps are and where my AI pipelines are,'” Thomas said.

Running the same Exadata hardware everywhere also takes the sting out of migration. AI projects are adding value to database migrations, and a like-for-like hardware move avoids most of the refactoring that once made them so painful, he noted.

“I’m coming from on-prem on an Exadata. I can move into the cloud on an Exadata,” Thomas said. “It’s the same hardware, same environment, same tools, same management, same performance.”

#5595. Carson Daly Has a New ‘Today’ Gig—Inside the Sprawling Long Island Estate He Calls Home When He’s Not in the Studio

Carson Daly’s weekends just got a whole lot busier—the “Today” host will join the Saturday edition of the show as a co-anchor.

The TV personality shared the news on the Nov. 5 episode of “Today,” noting that he’ll be joining existing co-anchor Laura Jarrett while upholding his weekday broadcast duties.

According to NBC News, Carson, 53, had been working as the interim “Saturday Today” anchor since September.

“I should just say, I’ve been very lucky to have a lot of TV gigs, but this one’s really special,” he said on the show. “At my age and at my stage of my career, to have an opportunity to come in and sit next to Laura and to learn and to get better at my job and be the best broadcaster that I can, it’s not something I take lightly.”

Nov. 7 will be Carson’s first official day as co-anchor.

“We’re going to have a lot of fun on Saturday,” he said. “But most importantly, the best part about the gig, like here during the week—which I’ll still be here during the week—is getting to go to your place of employment with such high-quality human beings. We are a family, and the fact that I get to spend one more day in this building, six days a week, is an absolute honor.”

When Carson isn’t spending time at the New York City studios that “Today” is filmed in, he has a beautiful family home in Manhasset, NY.

In 2013, the “Total Request Live” alum snapped up a six-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom estate for $6.5 million, according to The Sun. Carson purchased the home—which is about 25 miles northeast of Manhattan—for $6.5 million.

The Colonial-style abode is a gorgeous escape from the bustle of the city and includes a pool and a pool house.

Carson shared a glimpse inside the home in 2020, when he posted a snapshot of his family celebrating Easter. He noted that he was “especially grateful” for his family’s “blessings,” as he and his wife, Siri Daly, and their four young children virtually participated in their Catholic parish’s services next to a cozy fire in the living room.

“The Voice” host also shared some personal details about his sleeping arrangements with his wife, revealing they had a “sleep divorce” that was the “best thing that happened” to their marriage.

While his wife was expecting the couple’s fourth child in November 2019, Carson told “Today” viewers why the pair choose to seek out separate beds.

“I have sleep apnea, my wife’s pregnant, and during a home renovation, we downgraded to a queen-size bed. We just felt like we’re better off sleeping in different beds,” he said.

He joked that his CPAP machine makes a shared bed feel “like sleeping next to Darth Vader.”

“Most women would want to sleep in another bedroom,” he said. “I don’t snore anymore, but the noise of the machine keeps her up.”

In 2022, Carson confirmed that the arrangement continued after the baby was born.

“We both, admittedly, slept better apart,” he said on the “Today” show in 2022.

Siri is also part of the “Today” crew, where she works as a regular food contributor.

On social media, the chef and cookbook author often shares content from the family’s gorgeous kitchen, which has loads of cabinet space, sprawling counters, a subway tile backsplash, and even a “baking nook.”

In November 2023, Siri posted about her love of crafting intricate holiday tablescapes, joking that “no one is allowed to eat and mess it up,” while showing the tastefully decorated dining room.

#5594. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

#5593. Mortgage Rates Edge Down for Third Week

wood block of percentage change to UP and Down arrow. Interest rate, GDP, stocks market, financial, deflation and Inflation, ranking, mortgage, debt, Loan and Economic Recession concept

Mortgage rates came down for the third-straight week, but whether the recent trend is a sign of things to come remains unknown, although economists point toward any progress in a resolution in the Middle East as a step in the right direction.

The latest Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey® released Thursday shows the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 7.18%, down six basis points from 7.24% last week. The 30-year FRM is still up year-over-year from 6.22% last year. The 15-year FRM averaged 6.57% down from 6.60% last week. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.50%.

At presstime, the average rate was 7.17% Thursday afternoon, according to Mortgage News Daily, about one percentage point above year-ago levels.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said Tuesday’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey came in stronger than expected, with layoffs down slightly and a significant gain in job openings, which points to a potentially strong jobs report tomorrow.

“While solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term,” she cautioned.

Regarding Tuesday’s midterm elections which gave Democrats a majority in both the House and Senate, Jones said it is not yet clear whether the shift will be felt in the housing market.

“Many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead,” she said.

Although rates have eased over the last few weeks, they remain above 7%, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. Realtor.com’s October housing market report showed another month of a slowing housing market, with both buyers and sellers pulling back. Pending sales fell 10.5% year over year; new-home sales fell 0.6% on a monthly basis in September, which Realtor.com® Senior Economist Joel Berner characterized as “muted” for this year.

“Still, sellers aren’t delisting in droves, which suggests they are disengaging rather than acting out of distress,” Jones added. “With 43% of active listings having had a price reduction, buyers who can afford to participate are in a relatively strong position, facing less competition and more price cuts.”

#5592. What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12

Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?

This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.

“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”

During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)

OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.

“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”

OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.

“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”

Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.

“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.

Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.

“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”

At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.

“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.

KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.

“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”

Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA from Nov. 10-12. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.

We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.

During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.

#5591. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

#5590. Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Vows To Triple Homebuilding To Improve Affordability

Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has unseated the city's Democrat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after running a campaign centered on affordability and housing.

The Associated Press called the election for Raman on Thursday afternoon as she widened her lead over Bass.

Bass, 73, called Raman to concede her loss and congratulate her successor on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," the outgoing mayor said in a statement, in part. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."

The win underscored a "blue wave" that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

When Raman, 45, takes office in January, L.A. will become the nation's second-largest city led by a democratic socialist, following in the footsteps of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Raman's swearing-in will expand a growing roster of democratic socialist mayors nationwide, including Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC, Katie Wilson in Seattle, and David Morales, in Providence, RI.

Ahead of her victory, Raman appeared before a jubilant crowd of supporters at the Greek Theatre Plaza in Griffith Park Tuesday, arguing that L.A. voters were frustrated with Bass' record on cost of living and were demanding change, reported KTLA5.

"We watched friend after friend, family after family, leave because they couldn’t afford to stay here anymore. And we all talked about it as if these things were completely out of City Hall’s control," she told the audience. "That’s the cynicism that started to take over this city. That started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren't just bad, but they were permanent."

Raman ran a campaign focusing on housing, homelessness, and safety issues. The centerpiece of her platform was a plan to triple annual housing production by speeding up permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals.

Further proposals included overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to incentivize developers to build more starter homes.

""oday, less than 10% of the new homes built in L.A. are for-sale," Raman recently told Realtor.com®. "Under current city and state regulations, for-sale projects are charged higher fees, have a more-complicated approval process, are easier to appeal, and have increased liability risks for developers."

The 43-year-old councilmember was sharply critical of her mayoral predecessor, contending that Bass has not done enough to tackle L.A.’s yearslong housing crisis.

Bass’ record includes signing Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing, overseeing a historic rezoning program to clear a path for building half a million new homes, adding more housing units to transit corridors and job hubs, simplifying the building application process, and updating rent stabilization rules for the first time in 40 years to shield tenants from steep hikes.

However, it was on Bass’ watch that Realtor.com Metro Report Cards released in September ranked L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city—a result that Raman did not find surprising.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," concluded Raman.

Assuming a 10% down payment and a 6.5% 30-year fixed mortgage, a median earner in L.A. would have to spend nearly 85% of their income on monthly mortgage payments on a $1.12 million median-priced home, effectively putting ownership out of reach of all but the wealthiest buyers.

Beyond cost-of-living issues, Raman face pressure upon taking office to deliver on her lofty campaign pledge to reduce citywide homelessness by 50% in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

Fulfilling that promise will be a major challenge, given that recent 2026 data showed roughly 45,000 people living in tents and encampments on the streets of L.A.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5588. Same model, better answer: Enterprise data is what turns generic AI into a business tool

Generic AI models can write SQL, but they don’t know a company’s orders, customers or revenue definitions. Now, Oracle Database aims to give AI agents the context to move a stalled order forward.

But that shift raises questions about complexity, lock-in and security as AI agents start acting on live transactions. Oracle Corp.’s answer is a converged platform that keeps vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine, according to Hasan Rizvi (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, database engineering, at Oracle.

“If you ask a generic AI assistant, you get a generic answer,” Rizvi said. “If you ask an AI assistant that knows your business, you get a much better answer. Where is the stock? How can I fix the transaction? How can I expedite the delivery?”

Rizvi spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed database convergence and the safeguards needed for AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

AI lets teams spin up applications and data stores very quickly, making data sprawl everybody’s problem. Skeptics favor specialized databases for each workload, but new data types built inside Oracle’s engine inherit proven availability, security and scale, according to Rizvi.

“We’ve been working on this engine for 40 years, which is highly available, highly secure, highly scalable, highly performant,” Rizvi said. “If you build a new data type or a new workload in the same engine, you get all that benefit, multiple decades’ worth of investment.”

Choice is the other half of the pitch. The database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds, and Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, Rizvi noted. But security is where AI raises the stakes most, with Oracle’s Deep Data Security defining access policies in the database itself, so a user’s identity travels with every request from an agent or AI-generated app.

“Before, it took a lot of time and effort to find vulnerabilities to exploit them,” he said. “Now, with AI, it’s made it very easy to reverse engineer fixes for attackers to attack.”

#5586. Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson Reveal What It’s Like To Have 2 Celebrity Chefs in a Home Kitchen—and How They’re Prepping for Thanksgiving

Food Network chefs Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson are getting ready for another Thanksgiving celebration at their beautiful Hamptons home, and they've shared their best tips and tricks ahead of the holiday.

In an interview with People magazine, the power couple said that their best advice is to start dinner prep early.

“Prep as much as you can ahead of time,” said Williamson, 48. “I think stuffing tastes better the next day, once it’s had a chance to meld together.”

Flay, 61, dropped another helpful piece of advice: “Have chicken stock on your stove. It reheats the sliced turkey, which ultimately gets dried out no matter what you do. It can also thin out gravy that gets too thick.”

While one might assume that having two celebrity chefs in a household can feel like a case of too many cooks in the kitchen, the duo said it’s never a problem for them.

“We definitely split up the work,” said Williamson. “It never feels like we’re in each other’s way. It feels like it makes sense.”

Flay and Williamson invited the publication into the kitchen of their New York City home, showing off the gorgeous cabinets and generously sized island.

After a recent trip to Italy, the couple told the magazine that they’re planning a Tuscan-inspired feast this year, joking that it’ll be a “mini ‘Brady Bunch’” scenario with their blended families. Flay is dad to 30-year-old Sophie, while Williamson has a son, Hudson, 18.

In September, Flay spoke about the home kitchens he has in his two residences—his Tribeca pad and an estate in the Hamptons.

“The kitchen is spacious, and I make three meals a day in there,” he told The Wall Street Journal. ”The space relaxes me and allows me to cook for family and friends.”

In his home out East, the kitchen is not just a place to whip up delicious meals. The room functions more like a full-fledged restaurant.

“On the other side of my sizable island are three French cafe tables for guests,” he explained. The setup is even equipped with a professional fryer, which he described as a “recent kitchen splurge.”

Among his latest kitchen tools is a utensil he’s relied on for years: “I still have the chef’s knife I used at [the French Culinary Institute],” he shared. “When [I] prepare food with it, the feel reminds me that I’m still learning every day."

The kitchen of the Amagansett home is his favorite place to cook and where he has typically hosted Thanksgiving.

Flay built the dwelling from the ground up during his marriage to “Law and Order: SVU” actress Stephanie March. The former couple, who divorced in 2015, hosted a turkey dinner for a staggering 50 guests at their first Thanksgiving in the home.

“I prepared two 30-pound turkeys and cooked sides for days,” he recalled in a 2013 interview with Elle Decor. “I stand at my kitchen island from the minute I get out here to the minute I leave.”

Although Flay has publicly discussed his desire to steer clear of matrimony after three divorces, he and Williamson have agreed on an alternative way to show their commitment to each other.

“She’s like, ‘I just want a big ring and a big party,’ and I was like, ‘I love that idea because my marriages have not lasted, unfortunately,’” he told People.

Explaining that the “most important thing” is to “make sure that Brooke feels like she’s committed to,” he recalled of the moment he gifted her a “giant diamond ring” during a trip to London.

Williamson describes the flashy piece of jewelry as “the perfect ring,” adding that “it’s very sparkly.”

Although she was initially thrown off by the gesture, she now sports the rock on her right hand.

“I thought it was incredibly thoughtful,” said Williamson. “He said just because I don’t feel the need to get married or want to get married again doesn’t mean that you don’t deserve the big, beautiful ring that comes along with it.”

While Flay has been private about his past relationships, he admits he’s been more open this time around, and cites all they have in common for his “confidence” about their partnership.

“I feel very confident about this,” he said of the pair’s connection. “There’s so many wonderful things about it.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5585. Oracle wants to pull stalled AI agents out of demo mode and into production

Companies want AI agents faster than they can build the AI architecture to run them. Most can put together a convincing demo. Far fewer can move agents into production without exposing data, hurting uptime or blowing their budgets.

That gap is pushing database providers to rethink what a data platform for agents has to deliver. Nearly 70% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents, yet very few get them into production, according to Çetin Özbütün (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, data warehouse and autonomous database, at Oracle Corp.

“AI is very easy to demonstrate, but when you try to bring it into production, enterprises usually encounter four different deployment difficulties,” Özbütün said. “The first of them is around security. It’s very hard to securely provide access to AI agents, and that’s one of the top challenges.”

Özbütün spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI architecture and the challenges of moving agents into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Security is the first hurdle. AI agents are finding vulnerabilities at unprecedented levels, and customers often can’t patch their databases before attackers exploit those flaws, Özbütün noted. Oracle’s Autonomous AI Database encrypts data at rest and in transit by default, and users can’t turn those protections off.

“As soon as the vulnerability is found, before it’s released anywhere else, we bring it into production in Autonomous AI Database,” Özbütün said.

Resiliency is the next test, because agents run around the clock and put heavy, unpredictable demands on the data platform. Oracle commits to 99.995% availability with no exclusions. That figure is measured by whether a client can connect and run queries, not by whether the underlying infrastructure is running, Özbütün explained.

“We patch our systems on a weekly basis, for example,” Özbütün said. “All of our patches are online patches, so the database is up and running, accepting new connections, accepting new requests while we’re running the patch.”

The same always-current approach applies to Oracle’s Deep Trust AI architecture, in which the database enforces the security profiles that customers define. New capabilities such as the expanded Deep Data Security features show up in Autonomous AI Database as soon as they’re announced, ahead of on-premises releases, according to Özbütün.

“You do nothing as the user or administrator of Autonomous Database to get this functionality,” Özbütün said. “As soon as a new functionality is available, like Oracle Deep Data Security, it becomes available for you to use on day one.”

#5584. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5583. Active Inventory Grows as Sellers Keep Homes on the Market

As the holiday season approaches, housing market activity on both the buyer and seller sides are cooling right along with the temperatures. Moving toward what is typically a slower time for the housing market anyway, a new report shows buyers are holding back as elevated rates continue to diminish their buying power and sellers are bringing fewer homes to market, but not broadly delisting.

According to the Realtor.com’s  October monthly housing report, new listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest decline of 2026, while 4.4% of active listings were delisted, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The preliminary share of listings with price cuts was 20.5%, just 0.2 percentage points above last year and down from September.

Meanwhile, the report shows the number of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year, the greatest decline in nearly three years, as buyers pulled back.

“The market is cooling on both sides, but in different ways. Buyers are stepping back as higher mortgage rates cut into their buying power, while sellers are listing less often without a broad increase in delistings or price cuts,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “We’re seeing a pause in new supply, but owners who already have homes on the market appear to be largely unphased.”

The national median list price was $415,000 in October, down 2.2% from a year earlier and marking the 12th consecutive month of annual declines. Active inventory grew for a fourth straight month, bringing the national supply gap to 6.7% below typical pre-pandemic levels—the narrowest gap since the pandemic, according to the report.

Realtor.com says the stock of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year for a third consecutive monthly decline, the steepest annual drop since October 2023. Thirty-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, 110 basis points above a year earlier, putting added pressure on buyers’ purchasing power.

At the same time, 357,000 new listings came to market, down 7.5% from October 2025. Despite fewer new listings, active inventory reached 1,183,500 homes, up 7.4% year over year—the fastest annual growth in eight months. The year-over-year acceleration partly reflects a slower inventory comparison last fall; active listings have also risen each month since February. National inventory is now 6.6% below typical pre-pandemic levels, the narrowest gap since the pandemic.

Sellers did not respond to weaker demand with a broad wave of withdrawals, the report shows. The number of delisted homes rose 2.7% year over year, but the delisting rate— delistings as a share of active listings—held at 4.4%, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The rate ticked up from about 4.0% in September, in line with the typical seasonal rise into fall.

Price cuts remained common, but their share eased from September. 20.5% of active listings saw their prices reduced in October, down 0.3 percentage points from the prior month and 0.2 points above a year earlier. The October share was the highest for the month since 2022 and the second-highest of 2026.

“Rates eased to 7.24% on Oct. 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October, but they remained 107 basis points above a year ago and 53 basis points above early September. That loss of purchasing power is showing up first in demand: The stock of homes under contract is down over 10% year over year, while the rate of contract signings fell 17% year over year,” said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.

As the market moves into the holiday months, the balance between inventory and prices will be an important test, writes Realtor.com. More homes for sale and slower sales can increase supply, but if sellers do not make deeper price cuts, buyers may not gain as much ground as inventory growth alone suggests.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” said Krimmel. “New listings are down at a time of year when activity is already seasonally low, but the share of listings with price cuts is only 0.2 percentage points above last year and slipped from September. We also haven’t seen a meaningful increase in delistings. As we approach the holidays, a seller pulling a listing around Halloween or Thanksgiving is not necessarily showing the same distress as one who exits in midsummer.”

“A well-timed offer with reasonable, season-specific requests has a much higher chance of acceptance when winter is around the corner,” says one real estate pro. Read more.

#5582. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5581. Texas Man Admits to $1.5 Million Deed Fraud Scheme Involving Properties in 4 States

An empty piece of land might seem like an easy real estate investment opportunity, but for unsuspecting property owners across the country, those plots of land became targets in an alleged $1.5 million deed fraud scheme carried out by four men posing as the landowners.

Moshe Levi, 61, of Carrollton, TX, has admitted to helping carry out the plan, which involved impersonating property owners, arranging fraudulent sales, and laundering the proceeds, federal prosecutors announced this week.

On Wednesday, Levi pleaded guilty in a Boston federal courtroom to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The fraudulent property sales totaled more than $1.5 million, according to prosecutors.

Levi was one of three people indicted in July 2026. According to court filings, Levi and his alleged co-conspirators targeted vacant, unencumbered properties in Massachusetts, Georgia, Indiana, and Tennessee.

“Mr. Levi deeply regrets his conduct,” Levi's attorney, Ian Gold, tells Realtor.com®. “The plea represents an important step toward accountability to the victims and society.”

The scheme hit home for Halla Shami Jaraki, who owns a vacant lot on Mattison Drive in Concord, MA, but lives in South Carolina with her husband, Omar.

The couple had hoped to return to Massachusetts or pass the land along to one of their sons. Instead, their property was sold in 2024 for roughly $525,000 by someone allegedly posing as the owner, according to The Concord Bridge.

Developers began to build on the property but were stopped when the couple obtained an injunction against them. According to prosecutors, this couple’s experience was how the scheme worked.

Levi and his co-conspirators targeted vacant properties owned by people who lived out of state, then created email and internet-based phone accounts in the owners' names. They also obtained fake driver’s licenses and passports with the names of the property owners.

The group then used the forged documents and accounts to impersonate the owners of the properties and then allegedly persuaded real estate agents to list the properties, negotiate the sale of the properties, and transfer the deed to the unsuspecting buyer for payment.

The scheme allegedly extended beyond the fraudulent sales. Prosecutors said Levi and his co-conspirators moved money through individual and corporate bank accounts they controlled, using checks and wire transfers to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the proceeds.

Since around June 2023, Levi and others have shared or attempted to share in approximately $1 million in illegal proceeds, prosecutors said.

In April 2025, the FBI’s Boston office warned of an increase in deed fraud cases, with the rise of remote real estate transactions providing opportunities for “title pirates.” Property owners are being urged to be on the lookout for a number of warning signs, including missing property tax and water bills and sudden and unexplained increases in utility charges at vacant properties.

In a survey released in September from the American Land Title Association, 59% of title firms reported at least one incident of seller impersonation fraud in the prior year, which is more than double the 28% reported in the 2024 survey.

Levi will be sentenced on Feb. 11, 2027. He faces up to 20 years on each of the two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Prosecutors said they would recommend prison time “at the low end” of the sentencing guidelines, along with a fine “at the low end” of the guidelines, three years of supervised release, forfeiture, and at least $1.34 million in restitution.

Levi was charged along with Kyon James of Middleborough, MA, and Bradley Beauge of Somerset, NJ. Those charges for money laundering conspiracy are currently pending.

A fourth co-conspirator is based in Nigeria, but prosecutors have not publicly released their name.
