#5555. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5554. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5553. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, an Astra model built to keep vulnerability research in scope

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for authorized vulnerability research.

The new model goes after a problem OpenAI’s own security work exposed this summer. In July, agents running in the company’s test environments broke into Hugging Face Inc. while pursuing an assigned task. GPT-6 Cyber was trained to stay inside the targets a researcher has authorized, and the safety test OpenAI built for the launch draws on that incident.

That test, ExploitGym Honeypot, gives the model a difficult assignment and surrounds it with supporting services that are deliberately easy to compromise. Attacking any of those services counts as a scope violation.

With no deployment safety instructions in place, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds in 0.07% of graded runs. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6-Cyber, did so 5.51% of the time. Adding the instructions brought GPT-6 Cyber’s observed rate to zero.

OpenAI rates the new model at Critical, the top cybersecurity tier in its Preparedness Framework and the same classification Astra received at its September launch. GPT-5.6-Cyber had been rated High. The company says GPT-6 Cyber beats Astra on most cyber tasks, and an early research campaign on Firefox turned up 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla Corp. rated high severity. Mozilla has since shipped fixes for many of them.

Irregular, an AI security lab named in the system card, put the gap with Astra closer, finding the two broadly comparable apart from stronger GPT-6 Cyber results on long multistep tasks. Neither model got past fully hardened targets in OpenAI’s own challenge set.

GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cyber-specific model OpenAI has released this year. Like the first, GPT-5.4-Cyber, it sits behind an application process. Initial access is limited to a select group of approved customers in Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak program meant for offensive-style work such as penetration testing and red teaming. Those customers reach the model through the company’s application programming interface and Codex, and API requests have to come from approved networks by default.

Google LLC also put vetted defenders first when it launched Gemini 4 Argon in September. A week later Anthropic PBC rebuilt its Cyber Verification Program around three access tiers.

OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber will reach all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and GPT-5.6-Cyber is now opening to every customer in the tier. Critical infrastructure defenders get a Daybreak Red group of their own. On the defensive side, the company is extending early Astra access through Daybreak Blue to more organizations and to individual security researchers.

#5552. Rice breaks ground on the Arc in the Ion District, expanding Houston's innovation ecosystem

Nearly 200,000-square-foot research hub will connect Rice, industry and entrepreneurs to accelerate discovery, collaboration and commercialization

HOUSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rice University broke ground on the Arc in the Ion District, a nearly 200,000-square-foot research, corporate innovation and office building designed to bring researchers, industry leaders, entrepreneurs, investors and top talent together to accelerate innovation and move ideas from discovery to real-world application.

Located in Houston's Ion District powered by Rice, the Arc will feature seven floors of flexible, future-ready lab and office space for Rice and other organizations seeking proximity to leading research, highly skilled workers and Houston's dynamic innovation ecosystem. Rice will be a lead tenant, occupying nearly 80,000 square feet, or about 40% of the building.

"The Arc is a significant investment in Rice's future and in Houston's continued growth as a center for innovation," said Robert T. Ladd, chairman of the Rice Board of Trustees. "It will create new opportunities for industry leaders, researchers and students to work together on ideas with the potential for lasting impact."

The Arc will share a plaza with the Ion building, extending the 12-block Ion District and placing researchers in close proximity to companies, startups, investors and entrepreneurs.

"The Arc will bring Rice's extraordinary research and talent and Houston's impactful innovation ecosystem into even closer connection with the industries and innovators working to solve some of the world's most consequential challenges," said Rice President Reginald DesRoches. "That constant exchange of ideas and expertise will help move discoveries more rapidly from the laboratory to real-world impact."

Built for advanced research and collaboration

The facility will offer flexible lab and office environments that can adapt to evolving research and business needs. Floor plates will range from 28,000 to 31,000 square feet, with 15-foot floor-to-floor heights and infrastructure capable of supporting advanced HVAC, high-capacity electrical and emergency power systems and core laboratory requirements.

The building will also include conference and meeting spaces, an amenity lounge, fitness center, outdoor plazas, underground parking, secure bike storage and on-site retail and dining â creating opportunities to build solutions in the lab, develop partnerships across the district and connect informally throughout the day. The project is designed to meet LEED Gold criteria and will incorporate smart-building and energy-saving features.

"We are creating more than a high-performance business and research building," said Kelly Fox, Rice executive vice president for operations, finance and support. "The Arc is being designed as a destination where companies can access sophisticated infrastructure, connect with one another and build the relationships that lead to new ideas and opportunities."

Work within the building will span areas including artificial intelligence and machine learning, data science, robotics, quantum science and engineering, energy and more.

The groundbreaking event comes on the heels of the university's recent announcement of a transformational universitywide AI initiative to recruit 75 faculty members working across disciplines and expand AI-related courses and degrees. The initiative is accelerating Rice's emergence as a global leader in advanced computing and responsible AI.

"The closer researchers are to the people confronting real-world problems, the more opportunities there are to identify important questions, test ideas and improve solutions," said David Sholl, Rice executive vice president for research. "The Arc gives us an environment built specifically for that kind of sustained collaboration."

Rice's new AI Foundry will be located inside the Arc, where faculty AI experts will have offices and work with industry partners to tackle complex challenges, rapidly develop practical solutions and help organizations build long-term AI capabilities.

The effort will address a growing challenge: AI is advancing faster than many traditional industry innovation models can adapt. Instead of relying on lengthy, linear development cycles, the Foundry will bring Rice experts and industry partners together to identify high-value opportunities, design and test solutions, deploy them in real-world settings and continually refine them based on results.

The Foundry is envisioned to support organizations through AI readiness assessments, feasibility studies, proofs of concept, deployment-ready solutions, executive education and customized workforce training.

"The AI Foundry is exactly the kind of collaboration the Arc is designed to enable," said Amy Dittmar, the Howard R. Hughes Provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. "By bringing Rice researchers together with industry partners in a shared environment, we can accelerate the movement of ideas from research into practical applications while helping organizations build the capabilities they need to succeed as AI continues to evolve."

Responsible AI is a key catalyst in Momentous: Personalized Scale for Global Impact, Rice's strategic plan, which also calls for strategic faculty growth and specifically identifies cross-disciplinary cluster hiring as a way to build depth and breadth in areas vital to the university's future. The institution's four AI cluster areas are foundational AI; two applied areas including AI for health and AI for energy, the environment and resiliency; and responsible AI: society and ethics.

The Arc will complement the Ion building, the namesake centerpiece of Houston's innovation corridor and home to corporate and industry partners including Chevron, Microsoft, Aramco, ExxonMobil, Oxy, Shell, United, Transocean and Woodside Energy.

Co-working space in the Ion managed by Industrious is fully occupied, with more than 250 member companies. Activate, an organization that scientists and engineers become founders and move research toward commercialization, recently launched its third cohort of fellows. Twenty-five startups have participated in the program to date.

Companies based in the Ion, including Persona AI, CES Renewable, Greenflash Infrastructure and Cognite, also have experienced significant growth, reinforcing the building's role as a home for emerging companies and technology-driven organizations. The Ion's development also extends beyond offices and laboratories. MADabolic, a strength-training gym, recently opened in the building. Greentown Labs, Community Artists' Collective and Pickle Lab are also among the organizations that call the district home.

Together, the Ion and the Arc are intended to create a more connected environment where researchers, entrepreneurs, established companies and the broader Houston community can work, meet and exchange ideas.

"Houston has an extraordinary concentration of industry expertise, capital, talent and entrepreneurial energy," said Bobby Tudor, Rice alumnus and chairman of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative. "The Arc will help turn that concentration into action by creating more opportunities for breakthrough research to become technologies and companies."

The project is being developed by Rice Real Estate Co. Construction is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2028. Preleasing opportunities are now open for companies and organizations interested in locating alongside Rice researchers and joining the broader Ion District ecosystem.

For more information, visit https://www.thearciondistrict.com/.

About Rice UniversityLocated on a 300-acre forested campus in Houston, Texas, Rice University is consistently ranked among the nation's top 20 universities by U.S. News & World Report. Rice has highly respected schools of architecture, business, continuing studies, engineering and computing, humanities and arts, music, natural sciences and social sciences and is home to the Baker Institute for Public Policy and Kinder Institute for Urban Research. Internationally, the university maintains the Rice Global Paris Center, a hub for innovative collaboration, research and inspired teaching located in the heart of Paris, and Rice Global India in Bengaluru, India. With 4,793 undergraduates and 4,185 graduate students, Rice's undergraduate student-to-faculty ratio is just under 6-to-1. Its residential college system builds close-knit communities and lifelong friendships, just one reason why Rice is ranked in the top 10 for best quality of life by the Princeton Review.

#5550. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5548. CCM’s non-solicitation push tests limits of lender control

CrossCountry Mortgage has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, invoking two-year non-solicitation clauses and seeking payments for allegedly diverted loans. Attorneys say non-solicits have long existed but were often used as a deterrent because litigation is costly and proof is hard.   AI Summary

CrossCountry Mortgage’s enforcement of non-solicitation agreements is emerging as a test case for how far lenders will go to protect production in a higher-for-longer rate environment — a topic that has divided the industry.

The top-five mortgage lender has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, invoking a two-year non-solicitation window and demanding thousands of dollars in payments under their employment agreements, HousingWire reported Friday. CCM declined to comment on this story.

Non-solicitation provisions, which restrict departing employees from taking the former employer’s clients, referral partners or staff, have long been part of mortgage recruiting playbooks. But attorneys and executives say many lenders – mainly smaller ones – do not enforce them because litigation is costly and proof can be difficult.

That calculation may be shifting as origination volume remains compressed, margins stay thin and experienced producers become more valuable in a smaller market.

“With this high-rate environment continuing, top LOs will still be highly sought after, so they have to be careful on what type of agreements they enter into with a new company, what they own or not when they enter into those agreements” said Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson. “The companies hiring them have to be careful what they accept from the old company, if anything.”

Alan Pezeshkian, president of House America Financial, said every company has a version of a non-solicitation, but in practical terms, it’s more of a deterrent to the extent that companies enforce it.

“You’ll probably see that happening more now as volume has gone down, so companies have the time, resources and perhaps the need to make sure that they protect their organization and their assets. We have that clause but have I enforced it? No,” he said. “On one hand, you want to convey a message in the industry of where you stand. On the other hand, if you enforce it, you become a villain.”

“I still think that CCM was singled out for a practice that is common and widespread,” said Paul Hindman, an industry consultant whose clients include CCM, adding that the distinction between sending notices and pursuing a legal case is important.

To reduce the risk of these disputes, top or more sophisticated loan officers and ‘plug-and-play’ branches are increasingly negotiating exceptions that let them own the leads they personally generate, which are then carved out from the definition of company property. Other agreements spell out differences between in-house leads provided and funded by the lender and those generated by an LO’s own marketing, open houses or personal sphere, so those contacts can be solicited after a move.

Refinance opportunities often fall into the in-house category, because they typically come from the lender’s past customer database and corporate marketing campaigns. Several CCM letters reviewed by HousingWire specifically reference refi business.

That dividing line — who truly owns the customer relationship — is now at the heart of the recruiting and enforcement battle.

Brendan McKay, owner of McKay Mortgage, argues that originators hold the relationship, but concedes the picture changes when the company bought and supplied the lead.

“Threatening loan officers with lawsuits for continuing to serve clients whose trust they personally earned is not only anti-loan officer, but it’s also anti-consumer. It’s time for our industry to start writing employment agreements that recognize the difference,” McKay said.

One caveat: Hindman said employment agreements have expanded from simple two-page documents to “30 pages of legalese,” which makes it harder for loan officers to fully understand what they are signing. Still, he said, LOs cannot ignore contractual terms once they have accepted large financial packages to join.

“You can’t take a million-dollar sign-on bonus and say that you’re not going to do certain things, and then do those things and object to being called out for it,” Hindman said, adding that originators should be clear with borrowers up front when contractual restrictions could limit their ability to keep working together after a move.

Whether a non-solicitation clause can be enforced can come down to who is initiating contact and how the provision is drafted, with outcomes varying by state. Cases in which a loan officer actively reaches out to former customers are generally viewed more favorably for enforcement, attorneys said.

“But when the borrower is approaching the loan officer, that’s looked at a lot differently because you don’t want to restrict consumers – consumers have the right to choose who is going to do their loans, and you can’t go ahead and have an agreement that binds them,” said James Brody, managing partner at Brody Gapp. “When the borrowers reach out, I would have a hard time thinking that a court would go ahead and enforce that.”

Ron Gapp, founding partner at Brody Gapp, added: “When you start saying borrowers can’t approach somebody, it now is becoming a non-compete, and those are two different regimes. Definitely, a non-compete is going to have a lot more scrutiny than a non-solicit would.”

In the brokerage channel, some firms are rewriting agreements in response to LO pushback. Todd Bitter, national director of sales for NEXA Lending, said the company changed its contracts after new hires flagged language claiming ownership of their databases for 12 months after they left: “It’s not NEXA’s to own; it is yours because the loan officer should own their database,” Bitter said.

He described non-solicitation agreements as especially common among retail mortgage lenders, though some brokerages use them as well. Bitter also questioned whether lenders should rely on aggressive restrictions simply because they can.

“Is it legal? Yes. Is it right? No,” he said, adding that many cease-and-desist letters appear designed as scare tactics, even if they never lead to court. “But who wants to find out?”

The same tensions are emerging around referral partners. Some non-solicitation agreements extend to real estate agents and other referral sources, attempting to bar them from directing business to a departed loan officer. But, according to Brody, those provisions are on shaky ground.

“You can’t abridge the rights of third parties with regards to your contracts, and attempt to go ahead and stop those third parties from being able to have the freedom to use the loan officer or company of their choice,” Brody said. “This is something that would be looked at very sternly.”

A top mortgage broker who requested anonymity said the imbalance of resources between large lenders and individual loan officers turns cease-and-desist campaigns into “corporate bullying.” Major shops can afford to send repeated letters and pursue litigation if they choose, while former employees must weigh the cost, time and stress of hiring counsel or risking default, this source added.

CCM’s letter seeks repayment calculated at 75 basis points per loan for loans LOs originated that allegedly violated their agreements. Attorneys say that figure likely represents a rough estimate of the company’s lost economics — essentially the split CCM would have retained if the production had remained in-house, or a “haircut” on profitability. But they caution that originators need to understand exactly what any such formula is tied to.

“When you have a provision in a contract that acts as liquidated damages, you have to look at whether or not it’s a reasonable anticipation of those losses, with some facts behind it, or whether it starts to look like a penalty,” Brody said. “If it looks like a penalty that’s divorced from those specifics, then courts will routinely strike those down because you’re not allowed to have a liquidated damages provision that acts as a penalty.”

Brody also mentioned that switching the burden of proof “in and of itself would need to be analyzed and shouldn’t really be opined off the cuff.”

#5546. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5545. CFPB narrows enforcement practices, closes 86% of supervisory actions

The CFPB said it is narrowing supervisory and enforcement activity, closing 86% of open supervisory actions and cutting scheduled exams by about 50%. It is also reviewing ability-to-repay and mortgage servicing rules, along with revised fair lending and Section 1071 requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) said that it is narrowing its supervisory and enforcement activities and closing most of its outstanding supervisory actions, as well as pursuing changes to mortgage lending and servicing rules, according to its latest semi-annual report, released Oct. 27.

The report, which covers the first half of 2026, outlines the bureau’s efforts to align its work with the Trump administration’s priorities.

During the broader reporting period of July 2025 through June 2026, the CFPB closed 1,327 of the 1,552 supervisory actions that were open as of July 1, 2025, or approximately 86%. The bureau said the closures reflected either institutions sufficiently addressing the issues or findings that no longer aligned with its priorities.

The CFPB also reassessed all 80 open examinations and closed 66 that did not align with its revised priorities. The remaining 14 continued with a focus on correcting violations, addressing compliance weaknesses and providing relief to affected consumers.

The bureau also reduced the number of scheduled examinations by approximately 50%, shifting its attention toward depository institutions, activities it deemed actual consumer fraud and areas within its statutory authority. Mortgage origination and servicing remain among its supervisory priorities.

Under its new approach, the CFPB said examinations will focus on clearly identified products and potential violations tied to specific laws and regulations. The bureau also plans to avoid duplicating oversight already conducted by state or other federal regulators.

The CFPB is pursuing several mortgage-related regulatory changes under President Donald Trump’s executive order on promoting access to mortgage credit. Among its priorities is a review of the ability-to-repay requirements and qualified mortgage definitions under Regulation Z. The bureau is evaluating whether to modify the requirements, which apply to most residential mortgages.

The CFPB is also considering a final rule to streamline mortgage servicing requirements under Regulation X. The proposal, initially issued in July 2024, is intended to simplify the loss-mitigation review process and make it easier for servicers to assist borrowers who experience payment difficulties.

In July 2026, after the report’s primary reporting period, the bureau also issued a request for information seeking feedback on ways to promote access to mortgage credit.

The CFPB additionally finalized changes to its fair lending and small-business lending rules. In April, the bureau amended Regulation B, which implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The rule removed longstanding language supporting disparate-impact liability and revised restrictions on discouraging prospective credit applicants.

It also prohibited for-profit creditors from using race, color, national origin or sex as eligibility criteria for Special Purpose Credit Programs.

A separate May rule revised requirements for small-business lending data collection under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. Among other changes, it lowered the annual revenue threshold for businesses covered by the rule from $5 million to $1 million, removed certain data collection requirements and extended the compliance date to Jan. 1, 2028.

The bureau said it did not cite any fair lending violations during the reporting period, and that while it continued investigations, it instead focused its efforts on cases involving intentional discrimination with identifiable victims. It also made no referrals to the Department of Justice for potential patterns or practices of lending discrimination.

Overall, the CFPB said it closed approximately 40% of its pending investigations as part of its effort to align enforcement with its revised priorities.

The bureau reported receiving approximately 8.27 million consumer complaints between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. It sent approximately 7.5 million complaints to companies for review, and companies responded to 99.6% of those complaints.

The report’s complaint figures come as the CFPB has moved to limit the public availability of consumer complaints. In August, the bureau said it would stop publishing unverified complaint narratives and related data visualizations in its public database, arguing that the accounts present only one side of a dispute and may not reflect violations of law.

The bureau also said it would continue collecting complaints, reviewing company responses and sharing information with regulators. Previously published narratives will remain available through its Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) reading room.

#5543. Florida’s Amendment 3 could give housing market a ‘sugar high’ through year-end

Florida voters approved Amendment 3 with 62%, raising the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Agents expect accelerated buying and residency decisions ahead of the 12/31/2026 cutoff, with uneven effects by market and inventory type.  AI Summary

Jason Haber, a Compass broker licensed in both Florida and New York, believes the Sunshine State’s approval of Amendment 3 will lead to the state’s housing market experiencing a “sugar high” to close out the year.

Amendment 3, which was approved by 62% of the electorate on Tuesday, easily surpassing the 60% threshold, increases the homestead exemption, reducing the taxable value of a person’s primary residence in the state. Prior to this, homeowners could receive an exemption of up to $50,000, but the amendment increases the exemption on non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beyond that, the amendment says the exemption will be adjusted for inflation.

This means that if someone’s primary residence has an assessed value of $350,000, in 2028, the new $250,000 exemption would leave $100,000 subject to non-school property taxes, assuming the homeowner qualifies for the full exemption, generating potentially thousands of dollars in savings for homeowners.

Haber agrees that the amendment could create “serious property tax savings for those who homestead in Florida.”

“That was clearly very attractive to the majority of people. Affordability is the top domestic issue of our time right now and people see this as direct relief on their cost of living,” Haber said.

But the amendment comes with a caveat. Homeowners must establish primary residency in Florida before Dec. 31, 2026, in order to be eligible for the 2027 and 2028 exemptions. If you establish primary residency after the deadline, you will have to wait five years until you’re eligible for the expanded exemptions, which is why Haber believes the market may experience a “sugar high.”

“If you were on the fence this would certainly move you to act quickly,” Haber said, noting that Florida uses a variety of “carrots” to entice people to move to the state.

Chris Wands, the founder of The Wands Team, a RealTrends Verified ranked team, at Douglas Elliman, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, shares a similar view.

“It may make people move faster especially if they are already planning to move in the first half of next year,” Wands said. “I think it makes Florida an even more attractive state. A lot of people are moving here for the tax benefits, so adding another benefit helps with that.”

If a “sugar high” market does happen, local real estate professionals said it could have greater impacts on some markets than others.

“In Boca Raton right now, if a house is priced properly, you will have six people fighting over it, but that isn’t the case in every market. Further north in the state, the market is weaker because those markets are more impacted by high interest rates, so it would be a different story there,” Haber said.

Danielle Blake, the chief of residential and advocacy at Miami Realtors + RWorld, shares a similar view.

“Availability of inventory is going to vary by the asset class that you are looking for, whether it is single family or condominiums, and also the geographic location. In Miami, we have more condo inventory than single-family inventory at affordable price points, but that also varies by cities. Some cities have a larger supply, so it really varies,” Blake said.

In addition to a potential uptick in new residents, Wands also believes this could impact current primary residents’ decisions on purchasing larger properties, especially if they were previously concerned about how property taxes could impact their long-term affordability. This could then open up more mid-level or entry-level properties, helping more people get into the housing market.

Blake however, is skeptical, noting that despite this impacting the property tax portion of the affordability equation, many current homeowners may be reluctant to give up the 3% mortgage rate they have on their current property, especially in today’s mortgage rate environment.

In addition to this, property taxes in Florida are reset when a property is sold, meaning that if the purchase price goes up, so do the property taxes.

“Even if you’re not paying as much as you otherwise would have, anything that pushes up purchase price and, by extension, property taxes can have that adverse impact on affordability,” Haber said.

Additionally, legislators could increase the millage rate, which would hamper the affordability benefits homeowners are hoping to gain out of this amendment.

Beyond impacting homeowners, Wands also noted the amendment’s provisions relating to investment properties could also help renters.

Under Amendment 3, the annual cap on increases in the assessed value of non-homestead properties drops from 10% to 5%. This means that if a rental property’s assessed value is $300,000, the existing 10% cap would generally allow its assessed value to increase by as much as $30,000 in a year. Under the new 5% cap, that increase would be limited to $15,000.

“I think it puts guard rails up for renters and investment property owners by giving them more stability in what they can expect their taxes to be,” Wands said.

If Florida sees an influx of homebuyers set on establishing their primary residency prior to the Dec. 31, 2026 cut off, it would naturally have an impact on other housing markets as the buyers have to come from somewhere. Unsurprisingly, many are pointing to New York City as a market that could be impacted by the amendment’s approval.

“The year-end residency cut off is going to bring a lot of decisions,” Frances Katzen, the founder of The Katzen Team, a RealTrends Verified team, at Douglas Elliman, said. I’m going to be watching for people who are going to downsize their primary home here, keeping a small apartment as a base, but moving their primary residence to Florida. But that move doesn’t necessarily mean giving up a connection to New York.”

Katzen said she wouldn’t predict a mass exodus from the Big Apple based on this amendment alone.

“Buyers are not stupid,” she said. “They are going to weigh the full cost of ownership, including insurance, which is very expensive in Florida, along with maintenance and condo assessment fees, alongside family and business ties. This could influence the timing of a move but a property tax break alone won’t determine where people build their lives.”

On Wednesday, Florida’s Governor Ron DeSantis called a special session that will focus on some of the implementation language surrounding the amendment, so until then it remains to be seen exactly how this will impact the state’s housing market in the future. In the meantime, agents are prepping for a flurry of activity to close out the year.

“I’m getting a lot of emails and phone calls today from people asking about how they can qualify by the December 31 cut off,” Blake said.

What Blake is most excited about is how the amendment could impact future generations of homebuyers who have grown up in the state or lived there most of their lives, as it would immediately decrease the property tax portion of their housing affordability concerns.

While Amendment 3 could provide a short-term boost to Florida’s housing market, its longer-term impact will depend on how the tax changes are implemented and whether the savings are enough to offset rising home prices, insurance costs and mortgage rates.

#5541. Live – Is Trump Media Selling Bitcoin? Democrats Prepare Crypto Probe

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The company sent 4,259 BTC in two transactions, according to blockchain data tracked by Arkham. The coins came from wallets labeled as collateral for convertible notes, adding another layer of uncertainty around the Trump Media Bitcoin transfer.

The timing is difficult to ignore. Trump Media faces a potential $1 billion debt repayment deadline later this month, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize Trump’s crypto businesses. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

A November 2 filing also disclosed that noteholders can require cash repayment on November 30. If all eligible holders exercise that option, the company could face approximately $1 billion in repayments.

Trump Media warned that refinancing or other measures might not be sufficient. In that scenario, the company could be forced to sell Bitcoin or other digital assets to meet its obligations.

This disclosure gives the Crypto.com transfer a potentially more serious explanation than routine custody management. The company may be positioning assets ahead of a major liquidity decision. Although the reason remains unconfirmed, Trump Media could be selling its Bitcoin.

Senator Elizabeth Warren has pledged scrutiny of Trump’s crypto business relationships, while Representative Robert Garcia, expected to lead House Oversight, warned Trump-linked interests to prepare for investigations.

Democrats are expected to gain subpoena power when the new Congress begins in January. Reuters previously reported that investigations into Trump family businesses could begin as early as February.

The current political environment could complicate the outlook for Trump-linked companies. Congressional scrutiny may increase pressure on financial relationships, crypto holdings, and business operations connected to the president’s family.

So, is Trump Media selling its Bitcoin? There’s no clarity as of now, but a confirmed sale would raise questions if Trump Media is reducing its crypto treasury to meet financial obligations.

The next major date is November 30, when noteholders can exercise their repayment option. Investors will also be watching if the Bitcoin remains at Crypto.com, moves again, or appears in transactions that indicate an actual sale.

#5540. Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?

After a Democratic midterm win, lawmakers may try to ease drivers of inflation tied to oil, AI investment, tariffs, and jobs. The Fed is likely to respond mainly through how these factors move the 10-year yield and inflation expectations.  AI Summary

After the Democrats’ historic midterm win, the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump’s approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto?

Let’s look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy.

When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then.The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results.

Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms.

Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down.

This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates.

On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs.

Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off.

This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran.

For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates.

Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed’s focus fully on inflation.

One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates.

For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You’ve got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary.

The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there.

#5539. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5538. OpenAI makes new data center commitments, AI policy recommendations

OpenAI Group PBC today made a set of commitments designed to ensure that its data centers benefit the communities where they’re built.

It also proposed that lawmakers make some of the commitments mandatory for artificial intelligence companies.

The move comes two days after Democrats won both the House and the Senate on a campaign backing data center construction curbs. Additionally, voters approved dozens of ballot measures designed to scale back or limit AI infrastructure projects.

OpenAI today reiterated a commitment it made in January to fully pay for the electricity and grid upgrades that its data centers require. That covers items such as the construction of new overhead power lines. Additionally, the company pledged to provide “financial assurances” that will protect other grid users from potential project cancellations and delays.

It will also take steps to reduce grid strain. In particular, it will scale back its data centers’ power draw at times when energy demand is particularly high. That approach, which is known as a flexible data center model, has also drawn the interest of other industry players as Nvidia Corp. and Google LLC.

Some data center builders sign non-disclosure agreements with local officials to keep construction details under wraps. OpenAI today pledged not to use NDAs. It will instead only seek “narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”

OpenAI will publicly share construction plans and noise projections before construction of a new facility begins. Additionally, it will provide information about the jobs that each data center is expected to create. The goal is to help local unions and training providers prepare residents for the positions.

The company plans to tailor its commitments to each data center. It will publish the customized project terms in a document it calls a local compact. Once construction is underway, the company will provide annual updates and designate a local contact to field residents’ questions.

OpenAI hopes to codify some of the best practices that it published today into law. It released a policy paper that calls on lawmakers to limit data center developers’ use of NDAs and require them to cover their electricity costs. Furthermore, it argues that AI companies should be offered incentives to lower their power usage at times of peak grid stress.

Some of the best practices that the ChatGPT developer is prompting are already being adopted by other industry players. Google, for example, today pledged to fully cover the electricity costs of a new $17 billion data center that it plans to build in Wyoming. It will also finance related grid upgrades. Anthropic PBC made a similar commitment in February.
