#5536. Secure borders. A stronger economy. Washington must deliver both

The editorial calls for immigration enforcement that protects due process and lawful work, plus modernized pathways aligned to construction labor needs. It points to Harvard and NAHB data and urges homebuilding leaders to press for measurable policy outcomes on affordability and productivity.  AI Summary

In the first 100 days of the Trump administration, business leaders at residential construction and development companies were, in effect, summoned to the nation’s capital for an all-hands meeting with administration officials on housing affordability. The summons came on short notice, on a Sunday afternoon. The invitation carried an undertone. Attend or else.

The Washington, D.C., meeting never took place. But the episode captured the breakneck pace and take-no-prisoners approach of those early, flood-the-zone months. It also dialed in a distinctly unsettling tone for the rules of engagement between the new administration and the nation’s private-sector business leaders in one of the economy’s critical engines: homebuilding.

Now, following the 2026 midterm elections, those rules of engagement stand an opportunity to change.

Business leaders, including corporate strategists and their representatives on Capitol Hill, have a window to act quickly, elevate their priorities, and press for policy changes that have damaged or threaten to undermine some of the nation’s most important economic capabilities.

For homebuilding, residential development, and residential investment, immigration enforcement belongs near the top of the agenda.

The United States needs secure borders and enforceable immigration laws. It also needs the workforce capacity to build homes, grow food, manufacture products, and sustain economic growth. These are not competing national interests, and treating them as such has real economic consequences.

The question for President Trump, the incoming Congress, and the business leaders with a stake in the outcome is whether the next two years can achieve a more rational, workable balance among those objectives.

For the housing industry, evidence of what’s at risk is already accumulating.

Over recent months, HousingWire TBD has documented the increasingly disruptive effects of immigration enforcement on residential construction businesses and their trade partners.

Builders and contractors report job site interruptions, workers reluctant to report for work, and crews disappearing from construction schedules. In some affected markets, executives have reported reductions of 60% to 80% in available trade crews. These are accounts from specific businesses and markets, not nationwide estimates.

The disruption also extends beyond workers who lack legal authorization. Reports that U.S. citizens and legally authorized workers are apprehensive about reporting to job sites suggest that enforcement-related fear can diminish workforce availability and productivity.

Residential construction depends on the coordinated sequencing of specialized trades. When a framing crew is unavailable, subsequent work may be delayed, schedules are extended, financing costs accumulate, and closings slip.

For builders and their trade partners operating with already compressed margins and limited capital flexibility, repeated disruptions can pose a serious business risk.

These accounts do not establish that immigration enforcement has caused a nationwide construction crisis. They do, however, raise a question policymakers cannot responsibly ignore: Are enforcement practices achieving legitimate security objectives while imposing avoidable economic costs on lawful workers, responsible employers, and American households?

A study published on October 8 by Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that foreign-born workers accounted for 35% of the nation’s construction trades workforce in 2024, compared with 18% of the overall U.S. labor force.

Their representation is especially high in trades critical to home completion: 57% of drywall and ceiling-tile installers, 53% of roofers and painters, and 51% of flooring installers were foreign-born.

Harvard’s research found that foreign-born workers accounted for all net growth in the construction trades workforce from 2013 to 2024.

Separate NAHB research found that Hispanic workers represented 32.8% of the construction workforce in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2010. In Texas and California, approximately six in 10 construction workers are Hispanic.

Foreign-born status, Hispanic ethnicity, citizenship, and legal employment authorization are distinct characteristics. These statistics cannot be used interchangeably to describe immigration status. Nor do they, nor can they, truly reflect the full impact of foreign-born workers on job site capability and productivity because many undocumented frontline crew members are not counted at all.

The statistics, however, illustrate the industry’s substantial dependence on a diverse workforce, whose lawful participation must be protected.

Meanwhile, labor shortages are worsening despite reduced housing production. NAHB’s September 2026 survey found that, averaged across nine consistently tracked trades, 47% of builders reported labor shortages, up from 42% in April 2025. Framing shortages reached 57%, while finished carpentry shortages reached 58%.

NAHB also identified immigration-enforcement-related worker apprehensions as a contributor to worsening shortages, along with competition from other construction sectors.

Immigration enforcement did not create the industry’s longstanding workforce problems. Those problems reflect decades of insufficient domestic workforce development, shifting demographics, competition for skilled labor, and limited productivity gains. But making an already constrained workforce even less available cannot be a rational part of a national housing affordability strategy.

Washington does not need to start from scratch.

Bipartisan immigration reform initiatives have repeatedly recognized the need to combine effective border security, lawful employment pathways, immigration-system modernization, and solutions for established workers and employers.

NAHB’s comprehensive immigration reform policy, updated in November 2025, provides a practical foundation for the industry. It supports border security and effective enforcement, along with construction-specific visa reforms, legal workforce pathways, and domestic workforce development.

The association has also endorsed the bipartisan DIGNITY Act, which would strengthen border security while establishing conditional pathways to lawful employment for certain undocumented workers who meet defined requirements.

These proposals involve difficult choices and legitimate disagreements. They show that practical approaches exist beyond the familiar binary choice between unrestricted enforcement and abandoning enforcement altogether.

The remaining weeks of the current Congress and the next two years should be evaluated against three governing objectives.

First, the administration must enforce immigration laws while protecting lawful employment and upholding due process. Enforcement priorities, worker-identification procedures, and accountability mechanisms should minimize unnecessary disruption to legitimate businesses and protect citizens and authorized workers from improper detention or interference.

Second, Congress and the administration must develop lawful workforce pathways that reflect documented economic needs. That means considering construction-specific employment programs, modernizing immigration processing, and addressing established workers’ circumstances through clear eligibility, screening, compliance, and worker-protection requirements.

Third, immigration policymaking must elevate economic productivity and affordability as measurable priorities. Congress should assess workforce availability, construction delays, business costs and housing production alongside border-security and enforcement outcomes.

None of these objectives diminishes employers’ obligation to comply with the law, protect workers, invest in apprenticeships and technical education, or to improve productivity through innovation.

America needs stronger domestic workforce development and a workable immigration policy, not one in place of the other.

The industry’s responsibility cannot end with documenting the disruption and asking Washington for relief. Homebuilders, residential developers, investors, building-products manufacturers, trade contractors, and their associations have the evidence, economic standing, and organizational capacity to demand a coherent policy response.

NAHB has already established a reform framework and identified legislative priorities. Industry executives have documented the operational consequences, and research institutions have quantified the workforce’s dependence on immigration.

What, then, are business leaders waiting for?

The next step should be a coordinated, industry-wide agenda presented to the administration and congressional leadership, including specific legislative priorities, credible evidence of business impacts, and commitments to lawful employment, investment in the domestic workforce, and improved productivity.

Not another statement of concern. Not another round of partisan accusations. A sustained effort to translate widely acknowledged economic needs into workable policy.

The new political balance in Washington creates an opening, but divided government does not automatically lead to better governance. Progress will require leaders willing to negotiate, make difficult choices, and accept accountability for results.

The homebuilding industry should not passively wait to see whether that happens. Its leaders have both a direct business interest and a broader responsibility to help make it possible.

America should not have to choose between secure borders and a productive economy. President Trump and Congress should be held accountable for delivering on both fronts.

Not only should the homebuilding industry insist that it do so, but the industry’s leaders should strike with the same speed and ferocity the Administration used to kick-start its agenda almost two years ago.

#5535. webAI Launches webAI App for On-Device AI With No Per-Token Charges

The webAI app lets anyone build teams of AI experts that work across Slack, DocuSign, Hugging Face, Apple apps and more, while their files stay on their Mac.

AUSTIN, Texas, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- webAI today released the webAI app for Mac to the public for the first time. The app runs webAI's new small reasoning models on the user's own computer, so people can use AI on private work without sending files to the cloud or paying per token.

Most AI runs in the cloud, where usage is metered by tokens or capped by plan, and every document goes to someone else's servers. webAI runs the model on the Mac itself. A user can work through a sensitive client proposal or an unfinished business plan, revise it as many times as they want, and never hit a token limit.

"With the webAI app, we're making cloud AI optional," said David Stout, CEO and co-founder of webAI. "Why should you have to send a private document to an online service just to get help with it? Your Mac can do the work. You keep control of what you share, and you can ask as many follow-up questions as you need without watching a token meter."

In the app, users create Personas: AI experts with a role, knowledge and tools the user chooses. Several Personas can work together on the same task. A consultant could have one pull client requirements from project notes, a second draft the proposal and a third check the draft for anything missed.

Connectors work with the apps you already use, including Slack, DocuSign, Hugging Face and Apple apps. You control what each Persona can access and what actions it can take. A Persona can pull a client's latest decisions from Slack, see which contracts are still unsigned in DocuSign, and draft follow-ups for your approval. You spend less time hunting for context and copying details between apps.

Watch the demo: https://www.webai.com/blog/webai-launches-webai-app-for-on-device-ai-with-no-per-token-charges

Availability: The webAI app is available now for Mac at webAI.com.

#5534. NYC pied-a-terre tax notices get an appeals court green light

A state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had disrupted NYC’s pied-a-terre tax notice rollout, finding no standing or injury. A separate challenge by Steve Wynn and Wilbur Ross to the underlying state law remains pending.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration won another round on the pied-à-terre tax Wednesday, when a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had upended the surcharge’s rollout.

Appeals judges threw out an earlier Staten Island judge’s ruling ordering the city to cancel about 17,000 notices. They found the homeowners lacked standing and weren’t injured by the notices. All four judges agreed.

The surcharge is a pillar in the city’s plan to close a $12 billion budget gap. State officials projected it would raise about $500 million a year. The comptroller estimates the impact at closer to $1 billion before exemptions and appeals.

Wednesday’s decision does not directly affect a separate suit by billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn, former Trump administration Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife. They have challenged the state law behind the tax. That case remains pending in Suffolk County, with hearings scheduled in December.

A Staten Island judge had ruled Sept. 29 that the city skipped individualized decisions before mailing notices. The judge called the notices arbitrary and capricious and a due process violation.

Under the order, the Department of Finance was to cancel the notices and pull its roll from the agency website. New notices were allowed after an individualized review. Within hours, the city appealed and invoked a stay, so implementation continued.

Residential brokers told HousingWire TBD that the legal back-and-forth and the tax itself have had little impact on the owner-occupied market.

Ian Slater, co-founder and CEO of Trove Partners, said the market for under $5 million slowed in September and October. “We hit a record number of contract signatures above $5 million in September and October,” he said.

Wealth from a soaring stock market, plus nerves about its froth, is pushing buyers into top-end property, Slater said. Those buyers are “fully ignoring the pied-à-terre tax.” Some want second homes in New York City, he said.

However, listings of such properties remain scarce. Jessica Chestler, co-founder of The Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman, said bidding wars have erupted. Supply isn’t keeping pace with buyer demand, including for homes priced above $5 million.

“We recently represented a buyer in a bidding war that we ultimately won, but it required going $1 million over asking on an apartment that needed a complete gut renovation,” Chestler said.

Because the homeowners lacked standing, the court never ruled on whether the NYC Department of Finance’s rollout was lawful. The court said other arguments were either without merit or unnecessary to resolve.

Finance later used 2025 tax data to revise its determinations, the court noted. Several hundred owners learned they did not owe the surcharge. The surcharge covers only non-primary residences. Through July 2028, the measure impacts houses worth $5 million or more. Co-ops and condos face a $1 million threshold.

Wynn and the Rosses sued in late September. They argue the surcharge is an illegal property tax that discriminates against nonresidents. Wynn’s notice totaled $183,094.69, while the Rosses’ notice came to $83,531.52.

Trove Partners’ Slater does not expect the climate to change. “Political winds are clearly against the wealthy class,” he said.

He doubts judges or politicians will move away from the tax. “It’s definitely an annoyance, but it’s a bit of much ado about nothing,” he said.

AI-powered tax document extraction, reimagined client intake and an in-workflow Assistant help tax professionals spend less time on manual work and more time with clients.

FRANKLIN, N.C., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- This upcoming season, Drake SoftwareÂ®, a leader in professional tax preparation software, is putting more native AI capabilities to work right in the software that more than 70,000 tax professionals know and trust. With Drake SmartExtractâ¢ (beta), a reimagined Drake PortalsÂ® experience and an AI Assistant built into Drake TaxÂ® and Drake Tax OnlineÂ®, preparers can reduce repetitive work and focus more of their time on their clients.

Developed by Drake in conjunction with its customers, these AI capabilities integrate natively with Drake's tax preparation workflows and wider product suite. They are designed to help professionals move quickly to turn client documents into populated return fields and allow them to get answers instantly while working in a return, with the preparer firmly in control of all tax review and filing decisions.

"Tax professionals want time back during their busiest months, and they want technology they can trust," said Noha Ghazouani, Vice President of Product Management at Drake Software. "We're thoughtfully integrating AI into the familiar Drake workflows they already rely on, making it easier to get help with everyday tasks while keeping tax professionals in control. It's about supporting their expertise, reducing manual work, and giving them more time to focus on their clients."

Drake SmartExtract turns client tax documents into return-ready data

Drake SmartExtract applies AI to one of tax preparation's most time-consuming tasks: moving information from client tax documents into a return. Available in beta for Drake TaxÂ® and Drake Tax OnlineÂ®, Drake SmartExtract extracts data from supported documents and maps it to the corresponding return fields. Preparers can review and adjust extracted information before adding it to the return, reducing manual rekeying.

Drake SmartExtract will be available for purchase in December at $5 per return, with package pricing as low as $1.50 per return when customers purchase 100 or more returns. Pricing is subject to change. Visit our website for more information.

Supported documents include Forms W-2 and 1098; Forms 1099-B, 1099-DA, 1099-DIV, 1099-INT, 1099-K, 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC and 1099-R; Consolidated 1099 statements; and Schedule K-1 (Form 1065).

For Tax Year 2026, planned form expansion includes Forms 1095-A, 1095-B, 1095-C, 1098-E, 1098-T, 1099-C, 1099-G, 1099-Q, 1099-S, 1099-SA, SSA-1099, W-2G, 5498-SA and 5498 for IRA contributions. Planned expansion also includes additional Schedule K-1 data for Forms 1065, 1041 and 1120-S, including related supplemental statements.

Planned Drake SmartExtract enhancements for Tax Year 2026 include deeper integration with Drake Portals and Drake Workflow. These enhancements will help firms move client documents through preparation more seamlessly, focus review on items that need attention, and identify returns that are ready for preparers.

A reimagined Drake Portals experience simplifies client intake

Drake Portals provides the secure, client-facing starting point for tax preparation. Redesigned for 2026, it makes it easier for clients to upload tax documents, complete requests and communicate securely with their preparer. Its AI-powered document ingestion recognizes and then categorizes supported tax documents and connects them to the appropriate checklist items, reducing the time staff spend sorting through files and tracking what has arrived.

The newly launched Guided Organizerâ¢ helps practices onboard clients with customizable questions and personalized document checklists. Preparers can use a client's prior-year return to help tailor the intake experience, making it clearer what the client needs to provide.

Together with Drake SmartExtract in supported Drake workflows, Portals seamlessly connects document collection with tax preparation: clients upload their documents securely, AI helps organize them, and Drake SmartExtract extracts supported tax data for preparer review and direct population into the return.

An AI Assistant answers questions within the return workflow

The all-new AI Assistant is built directly into the return preparation workflow in Drake Tax and Drake Tax Online, where preparers can ask questions in natural-language chat. Using the screen they're viewing and information from the return, it answers tax questions, explains forms and alerts, clarifies how amounts were calculated, and suggests next steps. Preparers can get relevant guidance while continuing their work in Drake. A side-by-side view keeps the Assistant and the return visible together, so preparers can review guidance alongside their work without switching screens.

"Our focus is helping preparers accomplish more this season with the Drake software they already rely on," said Ghazouani. "These capabilities reduce manual work while keeping tax professionals in charge of the return and the client relationship."

Preparers should verify AI-assisted information against source documents and apply professional judgment before use.

#5532. American Housing Corp names leadership for new Austin division

American Housing Corporation launched in Austin with a focus on infill urban rowhomes. The company completed a “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized prefab system and is building a 250,000-square-foot Southeast Austin plant to produce up to 1,200 homes a year.  AI Summary

The American Housing Corporation launched an Austin homebuilding division and named three industry veterans to lead the new operation as it ramps up an infill-focused, prefabricated rowhome platform, the company announced this week.

Austin is the launch market for the company’s infill homebuilding strategy, which centers on designing, manufacturing and constructing urban rowhomes. The move comes as builders look for ways to add “missing middle” housing in supply-constrained, high-cost markets without relying solely on traditional greenfield development.

Parker Scott, a former division president at LGI Homes, was appointed general manager, Daniel Green will serve as director of construction operations and Luke Allen will serve as director of land.

Scott brings more than 20 years of homebuilding sales and operational experience to the role. Green joins from senior construction positions at Homebound, ATCO Structures and Perry Homes, where he focused on building operations and execution systems. Allen, who previously held land roles at Lennar and Ashton Woods, will oversee land acquisition, underwriting and pipeline development for the Austin market.

In October 2026, American Housing Corp completed its “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized, prefabricated building system. The company is building a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant in Southeast Austin designed to produce up to 1,200 homes annually, according to the announcement.

The factory-scale approach is intended to standardize production, shorten build times and provide more cost certainty, which could appeal to capital providers and municipalities looking for scalable infill housing solutions. For real estate investors and lenders, the combination of an infill land strategy with a controlled-offsite construction environment could change underwriting assumptions around cycle times and construction risk.

Alongside the Austin division launch, the company restructured its real estate operations and parted ways with co-founder Bobby Fijan. The firm credited Fijan with helping establish its early real estate footprint and championing urban, family-sized housing.

#5531. Five9 buys contact center intelligence startup Level AI after posting narrow earnings beat

Contact center company Five9 Inc. flexed its acquisitive muscles today as it announced a $325 million all-cash deal to buy an artificial intelligence-native rival called Level AI as it posted its third-quarter financial results.

The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Five9 is a leading player in the cloud contact center software industry, selling tools and services that enterprises use to manage their customer service interactions. Its web-based software spans traditional phone calls, video calls, emails, messaging, social media and other channels.

As for Level AI, it’s the developer of a contact center and customer experience intelligence platform that uses artificial intelligence to support human agents on calls and analyze, score and augment their interactions with the callers they serve. Its platform is designed to listen into customer service agent’s calls, so it can provide real-time guidance throughout and support workflow automation. The insights it generates can also be used to assist in agent coaching.

Level AI also develops autonomous AI agents that can automate some simpler customer inquiries and background operational tasks, freeing up human agents to focus on more complex customer issues. “Level AI’s AI applications help organizations improve agent performance, automate more customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn conversations into insights the whole organization can use,” Five9 said in a blog post announcing the deal. “Its applications are in production with enterprise customers today and handle more than 1 billion customer interactions a year.”

Five9 said it intends to continue offering Level AI’s applications as standalone tools for organizations that don’t want to shift their on-premises contact center operations to the cloud, also those who are using other cloud contact center platforms. However, it also plans to integrate the startup’s tools with its Genius CX Platform.

“As AI reshapes the customer experience landscape, we believe adding Level AI strengthens our competitive position, expands the customers we can serve, and deepens the AI talent behind our continuous innovation,” said Five9 Chief Executive Amit Mathradas.

Level AI founder and CEO Ashish Nagar said that by joining Five9, his company will be able to bring its applications and customer service-native AI models to thousands of new contact centers around the world, while allowing it to continue supporting its existing customers.

Investors don’t seem to have shared the CEOs’ enthusiasm for the deal, however, for Five9’s stock fell more than 23% in late trading after the deal was announced. That may be because of the cost of the acquisition. The $325 million cash outlay amounts to almost half of Five9’s current cash and marketable investments, which stood at $738 million at the end of the third quarter.

Five9’s results weren’t too bad. The company reported adjusted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $323.3 million, surpassing Wall Street’s guidance of 80 cents per share in earnings and $318.3 million in sales. But it’s notable that the company’s full-year guidance excludes any contributions from the pending deal, and so its value hinges on Five9’s ability to rapidly integrate Level AI’s technology.

For the current quarter, Five9 said it’s expecting earnings of between 88 and 92 cents per share on sales of $328 million to $334 million. But that guidance was mixed. Wall Street is looking for significantly higher earnings of 99 cents per share and $330.7 million in revenue.

For the full year, Five9 said it’s looking for earnings of $3.17 to $3.21 per share on total sales of $1.27 billion. Wall Street wants to see higher earnings of $3.26 per share on similar revenue.

#5529. RealPRO Select helps lift Realtor.com revenue

Realtor.com reported $160 million in fiscal Q1 2027 revenue, up 5% year over year, extending an eight-quarter growth streak. News Corp cited RealPRO Select expansion and broader RealAssist AI rollout as key drivers.  AI Summary

Move, the parent company of Realtor.com, said the momentum generated by RealPRO Select in fiscal year 2026 has carried over into the first quarter of fiscal year 2027.

During the first quarter of FY 2027, Realtor.com recorded $160 million in revenue, up 5% year over year, marking the segment’s eighth consecutive quarter of growth. These financial results were highlighted during News Corp’s fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday evening.

“In a housing market constrained by 7%-plus mortgage rates, Damian [Eales] and the team have exhibited exceptional discipline in their operational focus and AI integration, and that approach has converted revenue growth into meaningful bottom-line expansion,” Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, said during the earnings call.

News Corp executives attributed Realtor.com’s strong revenue performance to the growth of RealPRO Select. The company said it is focused on enhancing the platform with stronger lead generation, branding, productivity tools and training capabilities.

Realtor.com also focused on the expansion of RealAssist AI during Q1, including the launch of a pilot of RealAssist in Rich Communication Services (RCS), integrated directly into Google search and available on iOS and Android.

“The pilot is already attracting new users, driving strong engagement, and helping us capture pre-search intent earlier in the buyer journey before consumers ever enter a browser,” Damian Eales, the CEO of Move, wrote in a blog post about the company’s quarterly performance.

In addition, Realtor.com also launched RealAssist AI for Realtor.com+, which Eales said helps agents onboard their clients faster, build more tailored searches, summarize client activity and draft follow-ups in their own voice.

“The platform is already supporting thousands of successful agent-client connections, and early feedback on these AI tools has been very positive,” Eales wrote.

Eales also highlighted the relaunch of the My Home dashboard, which now includes a collaboration with Opendoor. Eales said this is encouraging sellers to engage a listing agent much earlier in their journey.

In addition, News Corp also noted that Comscore data shows 4.9 visits per unique user to Realtor.com, up 8% annually, and an average of 263 million monthly visits in the quarter, which the company said represents a “substantial” lead over Redfin and Homes.com.

Despite these strong numbers, Realtor.com noted that lead volume was down 11%, which the portal attributed to broader market conditions and its repositioning of customer acquisitions to higher-quality and higher-value leads.

“Despite a constrained housing market, Realtor.com’s strategy is delivering positive results, and we’re well positioned to grow as conditions improve,” Eales wrote. “Our focus remains on investing in our audience and AI tools that enhance a consumer’s experience and augment the role of the professional agent.”

Overall, News Corp’s digital real estate services segment generated $529 million in revenue, up 10% from a year prior. The company as a whole generated $2.28 billion in revenue, a 6% annual increase, and net income of $215 million, up 43% compared to a year prior.

#5527. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5525. Los Angeles votes all-in on housing, electing YIMBY-backed Raman

Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles as YIMBY groups framed the race around accelerating housing production. City timelines for statewide SB 79 transit oriented housing rules, currently delayed to 2030, are expected to face pressure under the new administration.  AI Summary

City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass to become the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, a win for the “yes in my backyard” groups that backed her challenge to the incumbent.

The Associated Press called the race Thursday. Raman, an urban planner and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, led by 4.2 percentage points, 52.1% to 47.9%, with roughly 76% of the expected vote counted.

She is the second DSA member to lead a major U.S. city. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani won a year ago on an affordability platform that made more housing a focal point. Bass conceded and promised a “smooth and seamless transition.” She is the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a reelection bid.

Raman won despite long odds. Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, retiring former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and nearly every City Council member backed Bass.

YIMBY Action, YIMBY Los Angeles and California YIMBY were among the housing groups behind Raman. Unions, progressive Democratic organizations, environmental groups and County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath also endorsed her.

Housing and homelessness drove the campaign. Raman pitched expanded medical teams for people in encampments and moving residents out of city-rented hotels into permanent housing. She said she could cut encampments by at least half by 2028.

YIMBY groups cast the race as a test of how fast the city builds. The movement pushes to ease zoning limits and speed approvals to expand supply.

“Her win in California’s largest city is a big moment for the pro-housing movement,” California YIMBY posted on social media.

One early test is how Los Angeles complies with Senate Bill 79, the state law that encourages more housing near transit. City ordinances that took effect June 30 hold off full compliance citywide until 2030. YIMBY advocates will likely press the new mayor and council to move that date up. Raman favored a quicker housing timeline.

Mayor-elect Raman could inherit a $20 million-plus liability if the city doesn’t approve Woodland Hills Country Club’s 398-home plan. The club’s attorney, Dave Rand, a Raman supporter, set a 60-day deadline, and the state housing department wants a response by Nov. 25.

Raman will need the council to do that. Most members backed Bass, so Raman must build a majority from a body that largely opposed her.

She will have allies elsewhere at City Hall. Controller Kenneth Mejia and newly elected City Attorney Marissa Roy, a DSA member, join her in what The Hollywood Reporter called a “triumvirate of progressivism” at the top of city government.

#5523. Autonomous combat drone maker Shield AI buys radar startup Echodyne for $5.3B

Defense technology startup Shield AI Inc. said today it has agreed to buy the Bill Gates-backed radar startup Echodyne Inc. in a deal valued at $5.3 billion.

The acquisition is intended to enhance Shield’s autonomous drone warfighting capabilities, it said.

Echodyne is a 13-year-old startup that’s best known for its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array or MESA technology, which is basically just a fancy name for its next-generation solid-state radar systems that can be integrated with a wide range of weapons and monitoring systems. The technology is designed to detect much smaller targets than traditional radar, including the kinds of compact autonomous drones that have terrorized soldiers on the battlefields of Ukraine and in other modern conflicts.

The deal comes just a couple of months after Echodyne landed a $250 million contract with the U.S. Defense Department’s counter-drone task force JIATF-401, which will see it provide drone tracking technology to the U.S. military.

Echodyne’s advanced radar systems look like a natural fit for Shield AI, which is the developer of the X-Bat and V-Bat vertical takeoff and landing systems, known as VTOL drones. Shield’s V-Bat hit the headlines in the last couple of years after assisting the U.S. Coast Guard in tracking down drug traffickers looking to bring illicit cargoes into the U.S. via speedboats, and notably participated in a number of large maritime drug busts. Shield AI is also the developer of Hivemind, an autonomous software system for piloting unmanned drones, as well as pilotless boats and spacecraft.

Shield AI Chief Executive Gary Steele said the deal will enable his company to accelerate its goal of branching into three different areas of unmanned systems. “We are building a new-generation defense technology company consisting of three fast-growing, high-margin, mutually supporting business units: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems,” he said.

Echodyne co-founder and CEO Eben Frankenberg said Shield AI is a natural partner for his company because it shares the view that autonomous systems must be able to sense their environment to achieve their desired mission outcomes. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government and commercial customers around the globe,” he insisted.

According to Steele, Echodyne will continue to operate as a standalone entity, as a separate business unit within Shield AI’s mission systems business. Frankenberg will remain with the company, where he will report to Steele as part of its senior executive team.

Echodyne is not going to layoff any staff, and nobody will be asked to relocate either, he said. In the longer term, the companies expect tighter integration of Echodyne’s radar systems with Shield AI’s drones.

The deal will see $4.8 billion paid out upon closing, with the other $500 million dependent on Echodyne meeting certain performance targets, which have not been disclosed. Shield AI said it was able to fund the deal with a combination of its own cash and a $2.5 billion cash injection that came via a Series H funding round led by Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase, which was also announced today.

Shield AI has a history of making decisive acquisitions. Its V-Bat and X-Bat drones are heavily based on technology developed by a company called Martin UAV Systems Inc. that it acquired in 2021. In June, it purchased Aechelon Technologies Inc., a developer of high-fidelity simulation and physics-based sensor modeling software, for an undisclosed price.

Steele added that the company may not be done with acquisitions, and will continue to look at making more deals in order to accelerate its growth strategy.

#5522. Compass boosts private listings while weighing Open Real Estate

Compass CEO Robert Reffkin praised the Open Real Estate initiative and said the company might participate. He emphasized Compass private exclusive inventory, 89,000 early listings on Compass.com and rising traffic, while the firm posted Q3 pro forma revenue of $3.90 billion and net income of $63 million.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin is not ruling out the possibility that his firm joins national residential real estate data-sharing initiative Open Real Estate.

“We welcome this change. It actually validates what we’ve been saying for the better part of two years, and so we are really excited to see the four of them lead in this way and to see others join,” Reffkin said during his firm’s third quarter 2206 earnings call with investors and analysts Thursday evening.

“In terms of joining or not, I think there’s definitely a path, but Compass International Holdings is definitely excited that there will be a national real estate listing service that will return the power back to the creator of the listing, the homeowner and their trusted agent, and that it’s good news for all agents and for all their clients, and we’re looking forward to seeing if there’s a way for us to be involved.”

Despite his praise for the initiative, which was founded by four of his largest competitors in the brokerage space and aims for fair and equal access to listing data, Reffkin also noted the growth of his firm’s private exclusive inventory.

As of early November, Reffkin said Compass had 89,000 listings on its site users could see on Compass.com prior to them being available to view on public listing portals. Additionally, Reffkin noted that in cities where there are no restrictions on the public marketing of office exclusive listings, on average this week, 63% of newly launched listings in the Compass brand employ its three-phase marketing strategy.

“We also hit over 70% adoption in some of these cities during the quarter, suggesting that as the industry’s artificial restrictions on homeowners and seller choice are removed, the good majority of listings would start off as a private exclusive or coming soon, and be a See It First listing on Compass.com and our sister company sites,” Reffkin said.

During the quarter, the company noted that traffic to its apps and websites was up 53.6% annually, according to data from SimilarWeb, and in September alone, after the launch of Compass’s new See It First offering halfway through the month, traffic was up 68% year over year.

“I would expect traffic to continue to increase as we’ve launched the See It First campaign,” Reffkin said. “The See It First campaign is also part of a rebranding exercise. I think some of our competitors have tried to brand the listings that we have as hidden but clearly, all of our listings are available to all agents and to all buyers. And when you call them ‘See It First,’ then it’s pretty clear we just want you to see it first on our site.”

In addition, building Compass.com’s inventory of listings comes with some added benefits in the AI-age. According to Reffkin, if you set up a search in a large language model (LLM) and ask it to alert you to any new listings in a given geography, “more often than not” it is providing consumers with Compass International Holdings listings.

“It is the new search alert, For anyone that wonders how are you going to find all the listings, if they’re not all in one site, well, Instinct and Muse prove that it’s just a different search alert. And it brings you to wherever the data comes first and whoever is the original author of the listing, which is obviously the listing agent, not a portal. And then they’re bringing you to listings that have more information,” Reffkin said.

This internal private listing network is also integrated into Compass’s Home platform, which the company is still in the process of rolling out to owned-brokerage agents. Company executives said that as of the end of October, they had successfully onboarded 33,950 agents. They expect to onboard the remainder of the 46,000 owned-brokerage agents by the end of 2026. Additionally, they said that they are on track to roll out the platform to all real estate professionals in their franchise network starting in Q1 2027.

By increasing the number of agents utilizing the platform, Reffkin said they are able to exponentially increase the number of client contacts within Compass’s database.

“We have 225 million unique contacts, and when you give me your listing, boom! It instantly pops up in their saved searches and I could then bring these buyers to your home,” Reffkin said.

Reffkin recounted the story of a Compass agent in Houston who had a client that wanted to relocate to Dallas. With Dallas being in a different MLS, the agent was unable to see MLS listings there, but within the Home platform, the agent could see all Compass International Holdings private exclusives in the city. According to Reffkin, the agent sent these listings to their client and the client ended up purchasing one that was listed by a Sotheby’s International Realty agent.

“That is a transaction that is across geographies and that would not be possible without the home platform,” Reffkin said. “That’s the power of the platform, where it is no longer restricting how people work, but creating much more flexibility and opportunity for the clients of our agents.”

In the third quarter, Compass International Holdings recorded an 11.6% annual increase in revenue on a pro forma basis, which assumes it had closed its acquisition of Anywhere on Jan. 1, 2025, to $3.90 billion. The firm’s net income came in at $63 million, up from a $4 million net loss a year ago. This marked the company’s first profitable third quarter. In addition, executives noted the company recorded a 6% annual decline in operating expenses on a pro forma basis.

“This was driven by the strong financial discipline that we’ve instilled into the organization over the past four years, and an acceleration of some cost synergy actions in light of the current environment. As of last week, we have actioned $360 million in net cost synergies compared to the $330 million full-year target for 2026,” Reffkin said. “We shared last quarter, and we remain fully committed to our $500 million-dollar target in less than three years.”

Reffkin also noted that the company is laser focused on agent attraction, retention and growth. The firm’s owned-brokerage operation closed the quarter with 85,476 agents, an increase of more than 2,000 agents from a quarter prior. This came as the firm lost 4,098 agents over the course of the quarter. But Compass noted that 58% of these separations reflected agents with $0 gross commission income (GCI) in the past 12 months — and 74% of separations reflected agents with $20,000 or less in GCI.

Owned-brokerage agents closed 140,118 transactions during the quarter with a gross transaction value of $138.9 billion. Franchise agents closed 191,809 transactions, totaling $108.9 billion in value.

Reffkin the firm expects to see further growth in agent count and productivity.

“The number of opportunities added to our growth team’s weekly active pipeline is up 39% quarter to date, compared to the second and third quarter of this year. Our walkover pipeline is also sitting at the highest levels we’ve seen year to date,” Reffkin said. “We believe the stronger recruiting pipeline we are seeing today is being driven by a flight to quality, as agents seek out brokerages that can provide them with technology and tools to help grow their business in a challenging market.”

Executives also touched upon the recent merger of mortgage joint ventures Guaranteed Rate Affinity and OriginPoint, which created a top-10 mortgage lender. The combined JV will operate under the OriginPoint brand moving forward.

During the third quarter, the total funded loan volume across OriginPoint and Guaranteed Rate Affinity was $3.30 billion, up 9.9% year over year on a pro forma basis.

Executives said a perk of now being a top-10 lender is that they have seen an uptick in interest from loan officers wanting to join the operation. Looking ahead, Reffkin said they want to be a top-5 retail lender.

“We’re obviously very committed to the business. We’re committed to ensuring that our real estate professionals and their clients are able to have everything in one place, which is not just technology, not just marketing, not just branding, but for title, escrow and mortgage as well,” Reffkin said.

#5520. In HelloNation, Excavation Expert Kenneth Zittel Explains Excavation Site Preparation Before Digging

The Feature Breaks Down How Excavation Contractors Research, Plan, and Stake a Site Before Digging Begins.

CONCORD, N.Y., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How do excavation contractors prepare a site before digging begins? A HelloNation article answers that question by walking through how excavation contractors research, plan, and prepare a property before equipment ever arrives.

The HelloNation article explains that excavation site preparation typically starts weeks before equipment reaches a property. Contractors review surveys, soil reports, and site conditions first, since that research shapes every decision that follows.

According to the article, a site visit usually comes next, with the contractor walking the property to check slopes, trees, and drainage patterns. These details help determine where equipment can access the site safely.

The article notes that utility lines must be located and marked before any digging starts. Locates are requested through a one-call service, giving utility companies time to mark gas, water, electrical, and sewer lines.

Soil conditions also shape the plan, the article explains, since different soil types drain and compact differently. An Excavation Expert studies these conditions closely, because soil behavior can also affect how well a septic system performs later.

Permits are another early step described in the article, particularly for projects tied to new construction or septic work. Pulling the right permits early keeps a project on schedule and helps it avoid delays once digging begins.

Drainage planning happens alongside this early groundwork, the article explains, since water has to go somewhere once a site is disturbed. Poor drainage planning can lead to flooding or erosion long after the excavation itself is finished.

Equipment access is planned carefully as well, according to the article, since heavy machinery needs room to maneuver without damaging driveways or walkways. The depth and reach of the equipment selected often depends on whether the project involves a foundation, a septic system, or utility trenches.

The article also covers staking, noting that marked boundaries protect trees, gardens, and fences while keeping crews inside the approved work area. K & D Development handles this kind of excavation site preparation as part of standard project planning.

Coordination with other trades matters too, since a delay in digging can push back schedules for framers, plumbers, and electricians. The article adds that weather often shapes timing, as rain and frozen ground can halt work for days.

An Excavation Expert typically builds flexibility into the schedule to manage conditions that are out of anyone's control, the article explains. Clear communication with homeowners throughout the process helps keep expectations realistic from start to finish.

Material deliveries are scheduled around this stage as well, the article notes, since gravel, pipe, and drainage stone often need to arrive before crews begin digging. Careful excavation site preparation at every step helps protect the schedule and the surrounding property.

The article explains that a final walk-through often happens just before equipment arrives on site. This step confirms that stakes, locates, and erosion control measures are still in place and visible.

Projects that involve excavation can feel disruptive to homeowners, the article notes, so clear updates throughout the process make the experience easier to manage. A contractor who explains the sequence of work helps homeowners feel more confident about what comes next.

How Do Excavation Contractors Prepare a Site Before Digging? features insights from Kenneth Zittel, Excavation Expert of Concord, New York, in HelloNation.

The proposed hard fork would zero the balances of four addresses linked to the Polymarket incident and one tied to Binance. Polymarket accounts for 23.86 million POL, while Binance’s address holds 46.63 million POL. The proposal would credit the equivalent balances to recovery wallets verified by the affected platforms.

Polygon block producers have already restricted transfers from the identified addresses. However, the current blacklist prevents movement without returning the assets to their owners.

The proposal would make the recovery permanent through a coordinated network upgrade. It would not create new POL or alter the token’s total supply. Governance discussion is scheduled for today. Approval would still require client development, testing on Polygon’s Amoy testnet, and coordination with validators.

The proposal describes the intervention as an exceptional measure tied to publicly acknowledged thefts and traceable funds. It warns that the action should not become a routine mechanism for reversing transactions.

#5517. Dropbox acquires Tigris Data for $350M, releases new AI productivity features

Dropbox Inc. is acquiring cloud storage startup Tigris Data Inc. for $350 million.

The company announced the deal today in conjunction with a major update to its product portfolio. It introduced DBX Agent Cloud, a service that artificial intelligence agents can use to store their data. Dropbox is also adding new AI productivity features to its flagship file sharing platform.

Sunnyvale, California-based Tigris Data offers an object storage service that runs across multiple public clouds. The company says that it enables applications to read and write several times faster than competing offerings. Furthermore, the service includes several features designed to optimize AI workloads.

AI agents often run in sandboxes that include, among other resources, the data they need to carry out their work. Loading data into a sandbox can be a relatively time-consuming process, which slows agent performance. Tigris Data offers a feature called bucket forms that speeds up the workflow. Furthermore, it prevents agents from modifying information that is used by other workloads.

Tigris Data’s service monitors the locations from which agents access records. When it detects a new location, it moves a copy of the records to a nearby server in order to reduce latency. The service caches the most frequently used files on high-speed storage infrastructure to further reduce access times.

Dropbox said Tigris Data will support its push into the AI infrastructure market. The company debuted its first entry into that product category, DBX Agent Cloud, in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Like Tigris Data’s service, it’s an S3-compatible object storage offering optimized for AI agents.

The storage stalwart plans to add a file system capability further down the line. Object storage is best suited for unstructured datasets, while file systems are used to store records that are organized into folders. Dropbox plans to release the technology alongside “content processing capabilities.” The company says that those features will make it easier for AI models to process information kept in DBX Agent Cloud.

The offering is rolling out alongside a major overhaul of Dropbox’s flagship file sharing platform. An enhanced search bar will enable users to look for images by entering a description of the file they seek.

Furthermore, Dropbox can now respond to questions about a file by generating a natural language summary. A worker could, for example, request an overview of the changes that colleagues have made to an important folder over the past week.

Dropbox can not only edit questions about files but also edit them. The company says that users can have the built-in AI models change a file’s format, move it to a different folder or combine it with other records into a PDF document. Several other actions are supported as well. Users can mix and match actions into multistep workflows.

The new AI productivity features are initially available to customers in the U.S., the U.K. and Australia with Standard and Advanced subscriptions. Dropbox plans to expand access next year.

#5516. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?

#5514. ANDPAD Named to "NextGen Tech 30 2026" as One of Asia's 30 Leading Next-generation Growth Companies

TOKYO, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ANDPAD Inc. (headquartered in Minato City, Tokyo; hereinafter "ANDPAD"), operator of the construction vertical AI "ANDPAD," has been recognized as one of Asia's 30 leading growth companies in the international awards program "NextGen Tech 30 2026."

Image: https://cdn.kyodonewsprwire.jp/prwfile/release/M108701/202610238598/_prw_PI1fl_kzb8jp1x.png

This award recognizes that ANDPAD's initiatives and growth in the construction AX (AI transformation) and DX (digital transformation) sectors were highly regarded in a multifaceted assessment of innovation, growth potential, and impact across Asia. The 2026 award recipients were officially announced at the Singapore Exchange (SGX) on September 30, 2026.

Since launching in 2016 as a cloud-based construction project management service, ANDPAD has grown into one of the construction industry's largest activity data platforms, utilized by more than 279,000 companies, and is now evolving into a vertical AI data platform. In recent years, as the use of the vertical AI "ANDPAD" has expanded at construction sites across Asia, particularly in Vietnam, ANDPAD has undertaken initiatives to improve operational efficiency across the construction industry's supply chain, prompted by business partnerships with enterprise companies.

In December 2025, ANDPAD launched the construction-focused AI project "ANDPAD Stellarc" and began developing and providing a suite of AI products, alongside an AI solutions business. ANDPAD is evolving as a vertical AI for the construction industry and for industries that involve new construction, maintenance, and repair of facility assets.

This award was granted in recognition of ANDPAD's development capabilities -- particularly in innovation and AI for the construction industry -- and its influence across Asia.

"We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the committee for selecting ANDPAD as one of Asia's leading growth companies. We received this award in recognition of the track record and strong growth we have achieved over the 10 years since the launch of our service. As the operator of a construction-industry AI data platform, we will continue to contribute to solving challenges and improving productivity not only in Japan but also across Asia, the United States and other regions through rapid AI development and customer support."

Reference: https://www.graniteasia.com/news/nextgen-tech-30-announces-2026-class-as-asias-ai-companies-move-beyond-software-into-the-real-world

NextGen Tech 30 is Asia's first major public-private initiative dedicated to recognizing and supporting top growth-stage technology companies across the region. Led by Granite Asia in collaboration with SGX Group, the program brings together sovereign funds, institutional investors, government agencies, and industry leaders to elevate companies with the potential to expand globally from Asia.

Granite Asia is a leading private capital platform in Asia that partners with visionary founders and business leaders to build industry champions. With US$11 billion in assets under management and co-managed capital, the firm has invested in 121 companies with valuations exceeding US$1 billion and has supported 70 IPOs globally. Investing across private equity, private credit, and public capital, Granite Asia combines deep technology expertise with flexible capital solutions to support ambitious companies as they grow, navigate key inflection points, and deliver long-term value across markets worldwide.

The cloud-based construction project management service with the top share of the market in Japan(*), ANDPAD enables the central management of everything from on-site operational efficiency to business performance improvement. Since provision of the service started in 2016, through associated development efforts that emphasize intuitiveness and ease of use and thorough support for implementation and utilization, the service has reached over 279,000 corporate users and 818,000 individual users.

ANDPAD was selected as a "2024 Recommended Technology" under the NETIS (New Technology Information System) by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism.

Details (Japanese only): https://andpad.jp/

(*)"Trends and Vendor Share in the Construction Business Management Cloud Service Market" (December 2025 MIC IT Report) (According to research by the Deloitte Tohmatsu MIC Research Institute Co., Ltd.)

Location: Sumitomo Fudosan Tokyo Mita Garden Tower 37F, 5-19 Mita 3 Chome, Minato-ku, Tokyo

Business Activities: Development, sales and operation of "ANDPAD" cloud-based construction project management service

Company Website (Japanese only): https://andpad.co.jp/

#5511. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5510. AI agents went shopping for TVs and laptops—and messed up nearly 50% of the time, study shows

As personal AI agents like Muse or Claude become part of daily life, more people are asking them to carry out shopping tasks. But there’s a problem: the agents aren’t very good at shopping. In a first-of-its-kind study, Visa instructed 22 different agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance—and, while some agents did significantly better than others, the overall success rate was only around 57%.

The results of the study are available on a new website by Visa that shows the outcome of 15 separate shopping expeditions by each of the 22 agents. Unsurprisingly, the agents powered by more cutting edge AI models fared best, with the Aragon 4 version of Google’s Gemini and the Wonder version of Meta’s Making notching the highest scores. Both agents made a successful purchase 82% of the time. A Claude agent came in third with a 76% success rate, while an OpenAI agent finished 6th with a 64% success rate.

The diagram below from Visa shows the performance of all 22 models. The vertical axis scores the agents’ success rate, while the horizontal one reflects the cost to run each shopping inquiry. (Visa notes that the five most expensive models succeeded on average 67% of the time, while the cheapest five scored 50%).

The agents’ struggle to make a successful purchase is rooted in part in a simple reality: The motivations behind any given purchase are often complicated and, in many cases, consumers lack information and are not certain what they want.

Visa’s experiment sought to capture this reality by, in the case of TV shoppers, assigning a list of attributes they needed in a television—for instance, compatibility with a child’s gaming console, a 30-day return window, and a model with Dolby Vision. As is the case with real world consumers, the purchaser (who in this case was also an agent) would volunteer some information, but not all of it.

The upshot is that, for an AI agent to succeed in Visa’s experiment, it had to interact with the shopper in a way that would elicit the missing information in a reasonable time. Success amounted to buying a TV that matched the shopper’s needs but, in many cases, the agents bought the wrong product, or simply failed to suggest something suitable at all.

“We’re not there yet from a trust or technology perspective. But we’ll soon get into a world where consumers can trust and delegate,” Visa’s Global Head of Growth, Rubail Birwadker, told Fortune.

Birwadker noted that agent-driven shopping is still in its early days, but that it is advancing rapidly. He added that the focus of Visa’s experiment—product discovery—is just one element of this new type of commerce that retailers and AI companies are trying to figure out.

For AI agents to enter the shopping mainstream, companies will also have to sort out smooth and secure payments—a challenge that Visa and its rival Mastercard are already seeking to address by educating merchants and building tools to facilitate so-called agentic commerce.

There are also new and unresolved legal issues when it comes to AI agents going shopping. Most notably, it’s still unclear who should bear the liability when agents make rogue purchases or commit fraud.

According to Birwadker, these questions will get resolved over time in the same way that an earlier generation of consumers and merchants learned to use ecommerce—he added, though, that agent-based shopping is going to be a very different experience than how we shop online today.

In announcing the results of its agent shopping experiment, Visa also rolled out a website that allows consumers to interact with the agents used in its survey.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5509. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.
