#5508. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

#5507. Apple and Home Depot join list of objectors to tokenized stock plan pushed by NYSE owner

An ambitious joint venture  to bring U.S. stocks onto the blockchain appears to be on life support. The venture, cochaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, and led by crypto firm OKX and the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, announced plans last month to offer round-the-clock trading of tokenized shares of 62 public companies. But as of Thursday, 54 of those companies had objected to having their shares traded on the platform.

Aerospace manufacturer Boeing and business software maker ServiceNow joined the objection list on Wednesday, a day after Apple, Home Depot and GE Vernova filed objections. Earlier objectors include some of corporate America’s biggest names, from Microsoft, Alphabet, and Nvidia to JPMorgan Chase and Walmart.

Home Depot declined to comment. Boeing, ServiceNow, Apple, and GE Vernova did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Companies outside OKXICE’s original proposed lineup have also filed objections, including Wells Fargo, Nebius Group, Arm Holdings, Cerebras Systems, and Cigna Group.

The expanded objection list comes a month after Cuomo announced the tokenized stock trading venue in a social media post. The venture was born out of a temporary exemption granted by the Securities and Exchange Commission in September that allows qualifying platforms to offer trading in tokenized stocks without registering as national securities exchanges, provided they meet certain conditions.

The eight companies in OKXICE’s original proposed lineup without a disclosed objection so far predominantly have ties to crypto or blockchain. They include USDC issuer Circle Internet Group, crypto exchange Coinbase, trading platform Robinhood, digital asset custodian BitGo, bitcoin treasury company Strategy and tokenization company Securitize. Software company Palantir and server maker Super Micro Computer round out the list.

OKXICE declined to say whether the growing number of objections would affect its planned launch.

The SEC approved the exemption two days after the Clarity Act, a bill to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate. Under the exemption, platforms like OKXICE do not need a company’s permission to offer trading in tokenized versions of its shares. Instead, they must notify the company and give it 30 days from receipt to object and block the listing, as Fortune reported earlier.

Applied Optoelectronics, a networking equipment maker among the companies to file objections, previously told Fortune that the new framework’s potential impact on its stock’s pricing, liquidity and volatility remained unclear. The company also expressed concern that investors might mistakenly believe it sponsored or endorsed the offering.

“At this stage, we don’t see a clear benefit to AOI or our shareholders that justifies these uncertainties,” a spokesperson said.

#5506. OpenAI’s Dots are coming up against the price of privacy, and the price of compute

Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue:

OpenAI took its Dev Day roadshow to London this week, attempting to sell the city’s developers on Dots, the company’s new, always-on AI assistant.

The company first announced Dots at its big annual developer event in San Francisco a month ago, pitching them as its flagship agentic offering. Whereas tools like Codex, the company’s coding assistant, wait for a user’s instructions, Dots are meant to be proactive. The assistant learns a user’s goals, watches their inbox and work tools, and starts tasks before they ask. (Dots aren’t available in Europe yet, but OpenAI said it is working with European regulators to change that.)

The industry is betting that proactive personal agents are the natural next step for AI, potentially driving as much value on the consumer side as coding agents did on the enterprise side. It’s an increasingly urgent new market for the industry right now, as companies, including Apple and Goldman Sachs, move to cap some employees’ AI spend, a trend that could dent revenue growth at the leading AI labs.

Given the stakes, it’s not surprising that OpenAI is arriving in a crowded market. Meta’s Muse got there first and has proved hugely popular with consumers; Elon Musk’s xAI has Grok Bot; and Anthropic has its own Duet on the market too.

How is OpenAI positioning Dots against that competition? By betting on high-end, high-spend users first.

“There are many other assistants out there, some of which have great UI interfaces, but what they can accomplish can be less advanced,” Romain Huet, OpenAI’s head of developer experience, told me. “We really wanted to nail the enterprise and pro use case first, because I think that’s where people will see the most value.”

That strategy also reflects how expensive these agents are to run. As my colleague Emily Forlini reported this week, Musk has said Grok Bot’s running costs are “unsustainably high relative to revenue,” and Adam Fry, who runs ChatGPT’s consumer business, told reporters that Dots are “on the compute-heavy side.” OpenAI is trying to combat this by routing some Dot tasks to Terra, a smaller GPT-6.1 model, instead of sending them all to the larger GPT-6 Astra, Emily wrote.

Huet told me OpenAI is aiming for token efficiency to keep costs down. He said the company’s Terra model can perform better than Astra in some areas, such as computer use and writing, at “a tenth of the price.” The company wants “the most amount of value delivered per dollar invested in these Dots,” he said.

These always-on agents also raise issues around consent, Whittaker points out. The people who email or message a personal assistant user, she argues, never agreed to have an AI read and ingest what they send.

“Muse is logging people’s contact lists, the people they talk to,” Whittaker said at the Masters of Scale Summit in October. “If you install Muse, and I am in your contact list, Muse now has my information. They are logging when we talk to each other…That could be extraordinarily serious for somebody working on human rights in an authoritarian country who is trying to communicate data with somebody outside of that country.”

“I personally said to my dot: I would love for you to categorize my email all the time. I would like for you to prep, possibly, what my answer might be, but don’t send any emails on my behalf ever, and don’t send any Slack messages on my behalf ever,” he said. “I want to do that myself.”

Ok, before we get to the rest of the AI news, I want to mention the amazing line up of speakers at our upcoming Fortune Brainstorm AI conference in San Francisco, which is taking place on Dec. 7 and 8. Come hear about the latest in AI from OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, AI luminaries Fei-Fei Li and Andrew Ng, and LinkedIn cofounder and Greylock partner Reid Hoffman—and that’s just to name a few of the many incredible builders, doers, and thinkers who will be on hand. I’ll be there, of course, alongside my Fortune AI reporting colleagues Jeremy Kahn and Emily Forlini. Why not join us? You can apply to attend here. And with that, here’s the rest of the AI news.

OpenAI hires Uber President Jill Hazelbaker to lead communications, filling a critical role that was curiously vacant for 10 months — By Emily Forlini

Dario Amodei wants ‘a country of geniuses in a data center.’ Realizing that vision requires risky financial mechanics, Anthropic’s IPO filing shows — By Wen Shao

OpenAI to change how it handles data center deals after backlash. OpenAI says it will avoid nondisclosure agreements when it negotiates data center deals with public officials, and will make sure local residents don’t pay for the electricity that powers its projects. The pledges are part of a new framework that OpenAI wants lawmakers to turn into binding rules for AI infrastructure. Under the plan, the company says it will pay the full cost of the power it uses, plus the grid upgrades utilities need to serve its sites. It will also publish water and electricity use for each facility, ask communities for input before construction, and favor low-water cooling. The move comes as opposition to data centers has hardened across the U.S. In this week’s midterms, voters backed restrictions on development in dozens of local ballot measures. OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, said the framework would help set “a very high floor” for how the industry moves forward. The company said it had been working on the changes for months. Read more in Bloomberg.

Anthropic’s Claude Code product lead jumps to OpenAI. Cat Wu, one of Anthropic’s highest-profile product managers, has joined rival OpenAI. Wu led product for Claude Code and later also took on Anthropic’s Cowork product. She left the company at the end of October, and this week she announced she will lead product management for OpenAI’s Core Products team. She will report to Thibault Sottiaux, who has led work on OpenAI’s coding agent Codex, Claude Code’s most direct competitor. “Together, we’ll build agents that have your back and your team’s, and keep you in control,” Wu wrote on X. Before joining Anthropic in 2024, Wu was a partner at Index Ventures. She became a public face of Claude Code as it grew into one of Anthropic’s biggest revenue drivers. Her exit follows the recent departures of two other Claude Code team members, including Anthony Morris, who built the Claude Code desktop app. Read more in Business Insider.

Apple cuts employees’ AI budgets. Apple is cutting how much its employees can spend on AI tools as part of a cost-cutting push, even as the company tries to put AI at the center of its operations. Last month, Apple quietly lowered the daily AI spending cap for some engineers to $200 from $300, and some teams could see theirs fall to as little as $100. Non-engineering groups, already limited to $100 a day, could see some caps drop as low as $25. Employees who need more can ask senior leadership for an exemption. Apple staff can use tools including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, and some teams are being steered toward cheaper or on-device models. The cuts come as new CEO John Ternus pushes the company to run faster and leaner, and after Apple’s R&D spending jumped 32% in fiscal 2026. Apple isn’t alone: Microsoft, Meta, Tesla, and Uber have all limited employee AI use as token costs add up. Read more in Bloomberg.

That’s how much enterprises spent on AI in the year to September 2026, according to Menlo Ventures’ latest State of Enterprise AI report. The figure is more than five times the $33 billion spent a year earlier, and growth sped up from the year before too. The number of companies paying for AI rose only modestly, meaning most of the growth came from existing customers spending more.

Spending also blew out budgets. The enterprises Menlo surveyed had budgeted nearly double what they spent in 2025, but on average ended up spending two and a half times that. The researchers say AI agents are driving much of the surge. On OpenRouter, a platform developers use to access hundreds of AI models in one place, agents now generate four out of five tokens, the units of text AI models process. A few companies also get the lion's share of that money. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google take more than two-thirds of enterprise AI deployment spending. Among businesses paying to plug AI models directly into their own products and tools, Anthropic now has more than half the market, up from 40%, while Google’s share fell by more than half to 9%. (Menlo Ventures is an investor in Anthropic and OpenRouter.)

#5505. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5503. How the Democratic party flipped the House and Senate, in 12 charts

The 2026 midterm race results saw a blue wave that secured a Democrat majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives. They flipped Senate seats in states the party hadn’t won in decades and took back a House that Republicans had controlled since 2023.

But what led to the turnaround that had voters turn out?

The Democratic party needed a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate, and many in the party had seen 2026 as a testing ground.

“What we’re seeing in the early parts of 2026 really puts Democrats in a good position, as long as we don’t screw it up,” Jen O’Malley Dillon, a Democratic campaign strategist, said at a Dartmouth political event in April. “It’s never been more complex to find a way to reach people. We are such a polarized country when it comes to our politics and, and, you know, people are tuning out in a lot of ways and for good reason—because we need to survive.”

In a stunning showing, Democrats flipped seven Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine.

Several of the wins came in what were once considered Republican strongholds. Kansas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 100 years, and a surge in turnout helped Democrats win across the South.

The Senate control means Democrats have an effective veto over President Donald Trump’s nominees for the rest of his term.

All 435 House seats were on the ballot, and Democrats went in holding 214. The party then went on to flip 25 Republican seats, and CBS estimates the party could reach 259 seats—well above the 218 Republicans held going in.

Wins came in battleground districts in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky, and Colorado.

Trump wasn’t on the ballot, but many voters treated the election as a referendum on him. Across age demographics, voters said their vote in Congress was to show opposition to Trump about 39% to 60%, while only 7% to 22% said they voted to show support.

The opposition vote was strongest among the youngest voters—60% of 18- to 29-year olds voted with intent to oppose Trump. Voters 65 and older were the most likely to say they were backing Trump (22%), but even that group leaned toward opposition. Trump himself claimed Republicans would have “won IN A LANDSLIDE” if he had been on the ballot, according to his Truth Social post.

Trump went into election day near the bottom of historical presidential approval. His most recent reading on the presidential approval rating sat at 29%, from Oct. 20. That’s the lowest for any president since George W. Bush fell to 25% in October 2008 during the financial crisis.

Democrats won every age group under 65. Voters 18 to 29 backed Democratic House candidates 72% to Republican candidates’ 25%—but they made up only 11% of the electorate. That’s a sharp turn from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.

The bigger gains came from the middle of the voting population. Voters aged 30 to 44 went Democratic 60% to 36%, and voters 45 to 64—the second largest group at 34%—went 51% to 47%. Only voters 65 and older, the largest group at 35%, narrowly favored Republicans 51% to 48%.

Concern about the economy remained a flashpoint among voters. About four in 10 named the economy as the most important issue facing the country—with the highest shares coming from Black voters (50%) and voters aged 30 to 44 (45%).

The issue a voter named as most important was a strong predictor of their vote. About eight in 10 voters who said the state of democracy was the top issue backed the Democratic House candidate, while immigration was the clearest Republican issue—89% of those voters backed the GOP. Both Democrat and Republicans were close to evenly split on the economy.

Many voters perceived that Congress is not doing enough to check Trump’s presidential powers. Among voters who disapprove of Trump, 94% felt that way. Voters who approved of him were divided.

But neither branch has much public trust. In July, only 4% of adults had a great deal of confidence in the people running Congress, and 53% had hardly any.

The executive branch fared slightly better in public perception, but it still had weak support. With both chambers flipping, Democrats now control what Congress investigates—as the majority now gives the party oversight on presidential powers.

The new Senate class includes several historic firsts: Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed will be the first Muslim U.S. senator, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan will be the first Native American woman in the Senate, New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas will be the first openly gay man elected to the chamber, Iowa’s Josh Turek will be the first Paralympian senator and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews will be the first woman elected to the Senate from her state.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. And in Texas, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton—ending a 38-year Democrat drought in the state’s Senate seat and overcoming Elon Musk’s $212 million effort.

Wall Street rallied overall following the midterm results. The S&P 500 was up 1.8% Wednesday morning and the DOW gained more than 1,000 points—but companies tied to Trump, Musk, and the AI buildout moved the other way.

Meanwhile, Trump Media fell 11.7%, adding to a 55% loss for the year. Musk had donated heavily to Republicans during the campaign, and both Tesla and SpaceX fell. Data center power providers took some hits as well: Vistra was down 9.6% and Vertiv 8.7%. Defense contractors including Lockheed Martin and L3Harris lost about 4%.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5502. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5501. The professions Americans trust the most — and least

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers earn the most trust in a 31-country survey, while politicians and influencers sit at the bottom of 20 groups.

A patient fills a prescription on a doctor's word. A parent signs a field trip form because a teacher vouched for the outing. A voter hears a campaign pledge and weighs whether to believe it. Each of these moments turns on a quiet judgment about whether the person on the other side deserves credence. Professionals shape the health care people receive, the schooling their children get, the money they save, the laws they live under, and the news they read. Most people cannot check that work for themselves. Few patients can audit a diagnosis, and few savers can inspect a bank's books. Faith in expertise fills the space between what people know and what they must accept, and it steers everyday choices large and small.

Public confidence splinters across these roles. Some occupations command broad goodwill, and others draw open suspicion. The divide runs through single fields and single institutions, where two jobs that share a label can land far apart in public esteem. A broad tag such as "business" or "government" can hide those splits, and anyone reading the popular mood through one catchall word risks missing them. Approval and doubt coexist. A single job can win praise from one slice of the population and scorn from another, and a tally of supporters on its own misses the balance between the two camps. Measuring how far trust outruns distrust, or the reverse, tells a clearer story about where each line of work stands.

Visual Capitalist ranked 20 professions and groups by that balance, using data from the Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index 2026. Ipsos polled 23,537 adults online across 31 countries, with fieldwork running from June 19 to July 3, 2026. Respondents judged whether each profession or group in their own country was trustworthy or untrustworthy. Net trust, the measure behind the ranking, subtracts the share who chose untrustworthy from the share who chose trustworthy and expresses the result in percentage points. A group that 50% of respondents call trustworthy and 30% call untrustworthy, for example, would earn a net score of +20. The figure captures the margin of trust over distrust. It does not represent the share of people who trust the group. A positive score shows trust outweighing distrust, and a negative score signals the opposite. Each of the 31 countries carries equal weight in the averages, so the results do not form a global estimate scaled to population. The published figures leave the countries unnamed and offer no results for any one of them.

Doctors claim the highest net trust of all 20 groups in the survey, at +43 points. They belong to the health and knowledge category, a cluster that also takes in scientists, teachers, and personal trainers. Among adults polled across 31 countries, no other occupation drew a wider margin of confidence over doubt.

A 91-point gulf separates doctors from politicians, who post -48 at the opposite end of the list. Visual Capitalist calls the distance stark. No two groups stand farther apart, so the doctor-politician pairing marks the full width of public opinion the index captures.

Skepticism toward politicians runs deeper than goodwill toward doctors. Politicians sink 48 points below zero, and doctors climb 43 points above it. The bottom figure outweighs the top one by five points in magnitude, which suggests the survey's harshest verdict carries more force than its warmest endorsement.

Doctors hold a 27-point margin over the armed forces at +16. Every group outside the health and knowledge category, from judges and police to bankers and journalists, falls behind physicians by at least that distance.

Personal trainers, a fellow health and knowledge group, register +10, a full 33 points beneath doctors. A shared category label does not guarantee a shared standing with the public. The health label cannot account for the doctors' edge, because a group in the same field lags them by a wider gap than the one separating doctors from the armed forces.

Scientists hold a net trust score of +42 points, one point behind doctors and second among the 20 groups in the survey. A gap of a single point at the head of the list amounts to a near tie. Adults across the 31 countries rate researchers almost level with the physicians who treat them.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers fill the three highest positions in 27 of the 31 countries surveyed, according to Ipsos. Four countries depart from that order. The trio's grip across so many countries shows the standing of scientists does not hinge on a few outliers in the combined average.

Teachers, the third member of that trio, trail scientists by five points at +37. The one-point margin separating scientists from doctors is a fifth the size of that cushion. The summit of the list plays out as a two-way contest, with teachers a step back.

Scientists stand 90 points above politicians, the group with the lowest score of the 20. Nearly the full spread of opinion in the survey separates the people who conduct research from the people who seek elected office.

This slide runs about 185 words, below the 300-word minimum. The source supplies only the scientists' +42 net trust score, their second-place position, and the Ipsos finding that doctors, scientists, and teachers hold the top three spots in 27 of 31 countries. It gives no reasons, country names, demographics, or trends for scientists, and no approved web detail covers scientists, so the slide stops where the evidence ends instead of padding.

Vocabulary flag: "trust," "points," "scientists," and "countries" recur across paragraphs because no precise synonym exists for the measure, the subject, or the survey scope.

Teachers carry net trust of +37 points, good for third among the 20 groups, and they finish 21 points ahead of the armed forces at +16. No other pair of neighbors on the list sits so far apart. Each remaining step between adjacent groups in the top 10 covers six points or fewer. The steepest drop near the bottom, from clergy/priests at -11 to advertising executives at -26, spans 15 points and falls short of the teacher divide. Advertising executives and government ministers, 11 points apart, form the next-widest pair.

The step down from teachers covers more ground than the entire climb from the first negative score, held by pollsters at -2, up to the armed forces. The 18-point stretch between those marks holds seven groups, counting both ends, including personal trainers, tech entrepreneurs, judges, police, and lawyers. Police and pollsters, whose scores straddle zero, sit seven points apart, one-third the size of the gap below teachers.

Teachers trail doctors by six points and scientists by five. The three Health and knowledge groups fit inside a six-point band at the summit. Below them, the armed forces post a score less than half the mark teachers earn. Teachers outscore the combined total of the three groups beneath them. The armed forces, personal trainers, and tech entrepreneurs add up to +31, six points under the teacher figure.

Shared category membership offers no guarantee of a high finish. Personal trainers, the fourth Health and knowledge group, land at +10, which leaves them 27 points behind teachers. The gulf between teachers and politicians, who sit at -48, stretches to 85 points. Government ministers register -37, the exact inverse of the teacher score. Educators enjoy a margin of confidence as wide as the margin of doubt ministers face.

Read together, the gaps describe a list that splits into a leading trio and everyone else, with teachers guarding the boundary.

The armed forces hold net trust of +16 points, the strongest showing of any group outside the health and knowledge category. Doctors, scientists, and teachers, the only groups above the military, all work in medicine, research, or education. The military is the first public institution on the list, in fourth place, and the only group beyond health and knowledge to reach double digits.

The armed forces open a wide margin over the three other groups that share the public institutions label. Judges and police each reach +5, leaving the military 11 points clear of both. Government officials and civil servants slip to -9, 25 points below the armed forces' mark. Across those four groups, the category stretches from solid confidence to outright doubt, with the uniformed service at its upper end. The spread shows respondents sizing up each arm of the state on its own terms, from the barracks to the government office.

The military's edge holds against every sector outside health and knowledge. Tech entrepreneurs, the best-rated business and finance group, post +6, 10 points short of the armed forces. Lawyers, the highest-scoring professional services group, sit at 0. TV news anchors, the top media role, fall to -3. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, register -11. Politicians, at -48, trail the armed forces by 64 points. In every one of those sectors, the best entry lands nearer to zero than to the military's mark.

Gallup reports that U.S. adults in its polling voiced more confidence in military veterans than in the military as an institution. The finding hints that views of the armed forces can hinge on whether people picture the organization or the individuals who served in it. Gallup's polling stays within the U.S., so it sheds light on one country's view of its military without speaking for the other countries in the wider survey.

Personal trainers carry a net trust score of +10, which hands the Health and knowledge category four of the five highest spots among the 20 groups surveyed. Doctors, scientists, and teachers claim the other three, and the armed forces stand as the sole group from outside that category to break into the upper tier.

Shared membership hides a steep internal drop. Trainers trail doctors by 33 points and teachers by 27, so they share a label with the most trusted professions without sharing their standing. The armed forces, at +16, sit six points above trainers, a gap less than a fifth of the one separating trainers from doctors.

Trainers build their work around individual attention. Personal fitness trainers assess a client's present fitness level, goals, and skills, then design individualized programs and track how the client progresses. Sessions may involve one client or a small group and can take place at a gym or in a client's home. Certification serves as a common entry requirement before trainers take on clients or coach members of a gym or health club. Employers favor certified candidates, though requirements differ from one facility to the next. Many trainers working in gyms and fitness facilities sell training sessions to members.

Trainers finish above every group in Business and finance, Professional services, Media, Religion, and Politics, along with three of the four Public institutions groups. Their cushion over the nearest of those groups stays slim. They clear tech entrepreneurs by four points and judges and police by five. Their +10 puts them 10 points above lawyers, who rest at zero. At the far end, trainers finish 58 points above politicians, who post the weakest score of the 20 groups. Among the four Health and knowledge groups, trainers post the sole score that falls nearer to zero than to the top mark.

Tech entrepreneurs hold net trust of +6 points, making them the single group in the business and finance category where trust outweighs distrust. Business leaders, bankers, and advertising executives all finish below zero. The nearest of them, business leaders, trails tech entrepreneurs by 14 points.

Adults surveyed across the 31 countries split the corporate world at the break-even mark. Founders of technology companies and the executives who run firms both earn their living in commerce, yet the two groups sit on opposite sides of the line. The ranking's authors flag wide gaps between jobs that share an industry, and business and finance offers a clear case. The business label on its own predicts little about where any one of its jobs will land.

Tech entrepreneurs share their stretch of the scale with public institutions and fitness work. Judges and police each post +5, one point lower, and personal trainers sit four points higher at +10. The sixth-place result leaves tech founders closer to the courts and law enforcement than to any fellow business group.

Their edge over distrust stays narrow. Tech entrepreneurs carry the slimmest margin among the six groups above +5. Doctors, scientists, teachers, the armed forces, and personal trainers all clear a wider gap between confidence and suspicion. Any reader weighing the business world's one positive score should see it as a modest win, far from the broad approval the top of the list enjoys.

Tech founders break a pattern among the groups with positive scores. Every other one comes from either health and knowledge or public institutions. No role in media, professional services, religion, or politics climbs above zero. Lawyers stop at zero without tipping into the plus column. Tech entrepreneurs stand as the one profession to earn net goodwill from outside public service and the health and knowledge fields.

Judges hold net trust of +5 points, a lead over their doubters narrower than that of any group above them on the 20-group list. Tech entrepreneurs, one spot higher, sit a single point ahead at +6. Personal trainers, a fitness occupation, draw a stronger result than the judiciary as well. The three health and knowledge groups at the summit enjoy a level of goodwill the courts do not approach. Judges outscore every media role in the survey, including TV news anchors, the strongest of the three. Respondents who call judges trustworthy outnumber the skeptics, yet the margin leaves the bench closer to the break-even line than to the top of the list.

Judges occupy the middle of the public institutions category, beneath the armed forces and ahead of the civil service. The armed forces, the category's strongest group, sit 11 points above the bench at +16. Government officials and civil servants trail judges by 14 points at -9, which puts them below zero. Three of the four public institutions in the survey hold positive scores, and the administrative arm stands as the lone exception.

Public confidence in the state tips from approval to doubt somewhere between the courtroom and the government office. Uniformed and judicial roles stay in positive territory, while the officials who run day-to-day administration draw more suspicion than faith. The courts sit a long way from political leadership, with government ministers and politicians both among the three lowest scores on the list.

Judges finish five points ahead of lawyers, who break even at 0 in the professional services category. The two legal roles hug the line where trust and distrust cancel out, one a step above it and the other resting on it. Neither commands the broad support the health and knowledge groups receive, and together the two courtroom roles sit nearer neutral ground than firm public backing.

Vocabulary flag: "trust" and "points" recur across paragraphs 1 to 4 of slide 7 as the name and unit of the measure. No precise synonym exists.

Police hold a net trust score of +5 points, the same figure judges post. Respondents placed the two groups on level footing, in back-to-back spots on the list.

Police also mark the final group above zero. Eight of the 20 professions and groups draw more trust than distrust, and police hold the last of those positions. Lawyers come next at 0, which leaves police 5 points clear of an even split between believers and skeptics. A cushion that thin means the doubters nearly match the supporters.

Public institutions show a wide internal spread around police. The armed forces sit 11 points higher at +16, and government officials and civil servants trail police by 14 points at -9. The four bodies stretch across 25 points, and police split the middle of that range with judges. An institutional label alone guarantees no matching regard from respondents.

Police still outscore most of the field. Every media role, the lone religious group, both professional services groups, and both political groups land below them. Three of the four business and finance groups trail as well, with tech entrepreneurs the only exception in that category. Apart from tech entrepreneurs, every group above police comes from the health and knowledge category or the armed forces.

Lawyers finish ninth with net trust of 0, which means the respondents who call them trustworthy equal those who call them untrustworthy. No other profession among the 20 lands on that dividing line between trust and distrust.

The neutral result turns lawyers into the hinge of the list. Eight groups above them earn more trust than distrust, and the 11 below them face the reverse. Negative scores outnumber positive ones, so a break-even mark lands in the upper half of the 20.

Pollsters, the lone other Professional services group, come in 2 points lower at -2. Neither member of the category climbs above zero, so a draw marks the best result Professional services can claim. Neither member of the category lands on the plus side, which puts Professional services alongside Media, Religion, and Politics as categories without a single group in positive territory. Health and knowledge, Public institutions, Business and finance, Media, and Politics all cover wider ranges between their highest and lowest groups. A poll estimates how people feel at one moment in time and makes no attempt to predict what comes next.

Courtney Kennedy of Ipsos suggested that anyone weighing a poll look for a named pollster with credentials and an open account of its methods. Stronger polls, she said, tend to lay out their procedures with greater clarity.

TV news anchors land 11th among the 20 groups with a net trust score of -3, the best result any media role posts in the survey. Distrust outweighs confidence for anchors by a slim margin. The score leaves them three points beneath the break-even mark that lawyers occupy at 0. Anchors are the second of 11 groups to fall below zero. Anchors sit inside a tight cluster of groups near zero. Pollsters score -2, one point above them, and business leaders score -8, five points below. Anchors outpace most of the business world, part of government, and every group in religion and politics. Their -3 beats business leaders, bankers at -10, and advertising executives at -26. Business leaders carry a net trust score of -8, which means more of the adults surveyed across 31 countries called them untrustworthy than trustworthy. Tech entrepreneurs, the one business role inside the top 10, outscore business leaders by 14 points. Respondents handed tech entrepreneurs a +6, the lone positive mark in the Business and finance category, and left corporate leadership in negative territory. Two roles from the same sector ended up on opposite sides of the divide between confidence and suspicion.

Business leaders hold second place among the four Business and finance groups. They finish two points ahead of bankers at -10 and 18 points ahead of advertising executives at -26. Their score sits far nearer the bankers' mark than the tech entrepreneurs' result. In the public's view, corporate leadership aligns with finance more than with technology. The four groups average -9.5, and business leaders hover around that midpoint. Outside the category, government officials and civil servants trail them by one point at -9. The near tie puts the people who run companies and the people who staff government offices on the same footing of public doubt.

The administrators rest nine points below the break-even line that lawyers occupy. Among the 11 groups with negative results, only pollsters, TV news anchors, and business leaders fare better. Civil servants carry the weakest mark among the four public institutions in the survey, and they alone in that category slip below zero. Uniformed and judicial roles stay in positive territory, while the civil service sinks into deficit. No single verdict covers every branch of public service in these results.

Politicians, at -48, trail civil servants by 39 points. Ministers sit closer to politicians than to administrators. Across these three roles, distrust deepens with each step away from public administration and toward political office. Respondents appear to reserve their harshest judgment for the people who hold political power. The staff beneath them receive a measure of leniency, though one that falls short of approval.

Journalists finish with a net trust score of -10, which leaves them tied with bankers and in the middle of the three media roles in the survey. More respondents doubted reporters than believed them, by a margin of 10 percentage points.

The tie links two groups from unrelated fields. Bankers come under business and finance, while journalists belong to media. Adults surveyed across 31 countries handed both the same verdict. Skepticism at this level crosses the boundary between people who handle money and people who handle information.

Reporters occupy the center ground within media, and no role in that category reaches positive territory. TV news anchors stand above them at -3, and social media influencers sink below at -44. Journalists land nearer the anchors than the influencers, which puts them on the less distrusted side of the media field despite their own shortfall.

Journalists fit inside a tight cluster in the lower half of the list. Five groups fall within 3 points of one another: business leaders at -8, government officials and civil servants at -9, journalists and bankers at -10, and clergy/priests at -11. Small differences separate institutions as varied as the civil service, the press, the banks, and the church. The five span four of the ranking's seven categories, from religion to public institutions.

A 14th-place finish puts reporters 53 points below doctors at +43 and 38 points above politicians at -48. Measured by that spread, the press sits closer to the least trusted group than to the most trusted one.

The bottom four groups, from advertising executives to politicians, all register -26 or worse. Bankers hold a net trust score of -10, so the share of respondents who call them untrustworthy exceeds the share who call them trustworthy by 10 percentage points. Thirteen groups post a higher score, and five post a lower one. Bankers fall in the lower half of the list, where every group scores below zero.

Bankers occupy the exact center of the business and finance category. Their -10 sits 16 points above the -26 advertising executives record and 16 points below the +6 tech entrepreneurs earn. The banking deficit runs less than half the size of the one advertising executives carry. Business leaders, at -8, finish two points ahead of bankers, and the two groups form a cluster of modest deficits between the sector's lone positive result and its steepest negative one. Three of the four business and finance groups land on the negative side, and bankers come in between the other two.

Bankers sit closer to the bottom of the full list than to its peak. They trail doctors by 53 points and clear politicians by 38. Every health and knowledge group outpaces bankers, as do lawyers at 0 and pollsters at -2. Each public institutions group beats bankers, down to government officials and civil servants, who hold a single-point edge at -9.

Bankers and tech entrepreneurs share a category label yet sit on opposite sides of zero. Adults surveyed across the 31 countries give technology founders a positive verdict and the banking trade a negative one. CNBC reports that analysts pointed to lingering distrust of banks as a main reason financial technology companies grew.

Bankers bear a deficit about one-fifth the size of the one politicians face. Doubt clouds the banking profession, yet it stays far from the depths the bottom three groups reach, each at -37 or worse.

Clergy/priests finish with a net trust score of -11, which leaves the lone religious occupation in the survey on the skeptical side of the ledger at 16th of 20. Doubt prevails over confidence for the people who lead congregations, though by a slimmer margin than the groups trailing them endure.

Religion forms a category with a single entry. Every other group on the list shares its field with at least one peer. Health and knowledge, public institutions, and business and finance each count four members. Media holds three, while professional services and politics each pair two. Clergy/priests stand alone, and the list offers no second faith role to measure them against.

Journalists and bankers each register -10, one point above clergy/priests. Government officials / civil servants at -9 and business leaders at -8 sit a notch higher. Five groups crowd into a three-point band from -8 to -11, covering 12th through 16th place. Pollsters, at -2, and TV news anchors, at -3, hold the milder negative scores above that band. Inside such a tight cluster, the order separating clergy/priests from their neighbors hinges on a point or two.

Advertising executives, at -26, open a 15-point drop beneath clergy/priests. Clergy/priests occupy the last spot above -20 on the list. Four groups sit below that line: advertising executives, government ministers, social media influencers, and politicians. Of the 11 groups under zero, clergy/priests sit seventh, with six gentler scores ahead of them.

Doctors sit 54 points above clergy/priests, and politicians, at -48, fall 37 points beneath the clergy. The armed forces, the highest-scoring group outside health and knowledge, stand 27 points above clergy/priests. Lawyers, at 0, enjoy an 11-point edge over the clergy. Clergy/priests finish 26 points ahead of government ministers and 33 points ahead of social media influencers. They land closer to the bottom group on the list than to the top one.

Advertising executives hold a net trust score of -26 points, the weakest result among the four business and finance groups in the survey. Tech entrepreneurs, the strongest of that quartet at +6, finish 32 points higher. Business leaders at -8 and bankers at -10 also clear the advertising group by wide margins, 18 and 16 points. Bankers, the nearest business peer, sit closer to zero than to advertising executives.

The fall from the middle of the table to this spot is steep. Clergy/priests, one place above at -11, sit 15 points clear of advertising executives. Across the eight groups from lawyers through clergy/priests, scores span a mere 11 points, from 0 to -11. No other pair of neighboring groups below the armed forces sits as far apart as clergy/priests and advertising executives. A single step down from the religious group covers more ground than that entire eight-group middle stretch.

Advertising executives finish 17th of 20, closer to the floor than to the center of the list. Government ministers, the next group down at -37, trail them by 11 points. Politicians, at the bottom with -48, sit 22 points lower. Doctors, at the summit with +43, stand 69 points above advertising executives. Of the 11 groups with negative scores, advertising executives post the fourth-deepest deficit. Every group beneath advertising executives belongs to politics or media, which makes -26 the poorest score for any group outside those two categories.

The business and finance category splits along clear lines. One of its four groups earns a positive score, two hover in the high single digits and low double digits below zero, and advertising executives sit far apart from the rest. Tech entrepreneurs, by contrast, stand closer to the armed forces than to advertising executives. On this scale, respondents treat advertising executives as closer kin to political leadership than to the bankers, business leaders, and tech entrepreneurs who share their category.

Government ministers carry a net trust score of -37 points, the third-worst result among the 20 groups. Doubters outnumber believers by a wide margin, and two groups alone fare worse.

Advertising executives, the next group up the table, score -26. The 11-point slide from that business role to ministers marks the second-largest step between neighboring groups in the bottom half of the list. Only the gap separating clergy/priests from advertising executives runs wider. Every business and finance group, bankers and advertising executives included, earns a milder verdict than the people holding ministerial posts. Business leaders, at -8, stand 29 points ahead of ministers.

Each of the four public institutions in the survey finishes above ministers. The armed forces, judges, and police all hold positive scores, and ministers trail each by more than 40 points. The armed forces, at +16, sit 53 points higher. Judges and police, tied at +5, clear ministers by 42 points.

Politics claims two of the three spots at the foot of the list. Ministers share the category with politicians, who sit 11 points lower at -48. Social media influencers, at -44, land between the two political groups and trail ministers by seven points.

Ministers draw a harsher verdict than every media role except influencers. TV news anchors, the strongest media role at -3, rise 34 points above ministers, and journalists, at -10, sit 27 points clear. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, hold a 26-point edge at -11.

Ministers sit 37 points below lawyers, whose score of zero marks the line where trust and distrust balance. Pollsters, one notch below that line at -2, outscore ministers by 35 points. The distance to doctors at the opposite end stretches to 80 points.

No other category in the table keeps every member below -30, so politics stands as the one field where skepticism reaches each role it contains.

Social media influencers post a net trust score of -44, the second-weakest result among the 20 professions and the poorest for any group outside politics. Only politicians land beneath them. Government ministers, the other political group near the bottom, finish 7 points higher at -37.

Influencers trail the other two media roles by a wide margin. TV news anchors score -3 and journalists -10, which leaves influencers 41 points behind anchors and 34 behind journalists. Visual Capitalist reads this spread as a sign of a major divide in how people view different media roles.

No other grouping in the survey stretches as far from its best member to its worst. Media jobs land at 11th, 14th, and 19th in the 20-group list. The government split between civil servants and ministers, the other sharp gap the source flags inside government, covers less ground than the distance separating anchors from influencers. Averaging the three roles into one media figure would mask the rift, landing at a number that describes none of them.

The influencer deficit runs more than four times as deep as the journalists' and more than 14 times as deep as the anchors'. Distrust outweighs trust for all three media roles, yet the shortfall for the two news jobs looks modest beside the hole influencers face. Anchors and journalists hover within reach of the break-even mark. Influencers, by contrast, sit within sight of the scale's floor.

Advertising executives, at -26 the lowest business and finance score, finish 18 points clear of influencers. Clergy/priests at -11 and bankers at -10 sit more than 30 points above them. Doctors, at +43, hold an 87-point edge. Every business group, every public institution, and the lone religious role outscore influencers.

Respondents place influencers nearer to politicians and ministers than to the anchors and journalists who share their field.

Politicians finish with a net score of -48 points, the weakest of all 20 groups, after 13% of respondents called them trustworthy against 61% who called them untrustworthy.

Skeptics outnumber believers by close to five to one. Each respondent who vouched for politicians stood alongside about 4.7 who dismissed them. The 61% figure also forms an outright majority, so more than half of everyone surveyed put politicians in the untrustworthy column. Politicians are the only group whose separate trustworthy and untrustworthy shares appear in the published results. Their -48 is the one score on the list readers can break into its two parts.

The two shares account for 74% of respondents. The other 26% landed in neither camp and offered no verdict either way. Those uncommitted respondents form the only pool politicians could win over without changing anyone's mind.

Politics posts the poorest average of the seven categories, at -42.5 across its two groups. Media comes next at -19 for its three roles, leaving the political category 23.5 points behind the second-worst field. Social media influencers account for most of that media deficit, pulling the category below the scores of TV news anchors and journalists, two roles that sit far closer to neutral. Politics has no such buffer. Its other group, government ministers, also draws heavy distrust. Influencers, at -44, still sit four points above politicians and form the politicians' closest neighbor on the list.

Politicians would remain in negative territory if every one of the uncommitted 26% swung to their side. Their trustworthy share would climb to 39%, leaving them 22 points shy of the 61% who distrust them. An even score would require 24% of respondents to cross from distrust to trust, leaving both shares at 37%. Any path to a positive score runs through people who have written politicians off.

#5500. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5499. Wall Street’s best post-midterm rally in 44 years lasted just one day—then $3 trillion vanished as chip stocks plunged over AI fears

The Nasdaq fell about 5% on Thursday and the S&P 500 nearly 4%, just a day after Wall Street had cheered the Democratic sweep of Congress.

By early Thursday afternoon, the Nasdaq dropped 5.2% and the S&P 500 3.8%, and the Dow was down 2.9%, or more than 1,500 points. The S&P 500 fell as low as 7,394.49, below where it closed on Election Day. Thursday’s drop off seemed to hit AI and tech stocks the hardest: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down about 9.75% in a Reuters intraday snapshot and briefly fell as much as 11%, on track for its steepest daily loss since March 2020. Among other AI-related stocks include AMD and Micron, which each lost roughly 15%, and Nvidia fell almost 9%.

But the drop came a day late. On Wednesday, the Dow rose 1,569 points, or 3%, its best performance after a midterm election in 44 years. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,688.62, as oil fell more than 8% and investors seemed to hope that a divided government would mean steadier policy.

But by Thursday, U.S. stocks had shed roughly $3 trillion in market value, and the Dow was heading for its worst second trading day after a midterm in data going back to the index’s start in 1896.

Perhaps part of the reason for the huge hit to the AI and tech sectors could be because of the Blue Tsunami. There were 41 ballot measures regarding slowing down data center buildouts, and most of them passed, especially in Ohio. So the midterm risk to AI was showing up on Wednesday, but only in parts of the market, before it showed up in full Thursday.

Vistra plunged 14% and Vertiv fell 13% on fears of data center moratoriums, while Nvidia slipped only 3% on Wednesday. Smaller AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave were also hit hard, since a permitting slowdown in Texas would hurt operators like CoreWeave before it reached the hyperscalers that are their main customers. Meanwhile, some of the biggest tech companies—which pay for the build-out—saw their stocks rise. Some analysts and economists argued political pushback could let air out of an inevitable AI bubble without popping it.

That’s when Asian markets started selling off overnight: South Korea’s Kospi closed down 5.28% with trading halts during the session, Taiwan’s main index fell 3.2% and the Nikkei 1.79%. By Thursday, the largest U.S. tech names had joined the decline: Tesla dropped as much as 10%, Qualcomm fell 11.2% and Arm Holdings 11% after weaker technology earnings. Oil prices also rebounded following Wednesday’s drop.

While the losses were most concentrated in tech, four of the S&P 500’s 11 sectors were up on the day, including consumer staples, which rose 1.5%, and Berkshire Hathaway hit an all-time high.

Texas is the main source of worry about the build-out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants an immediate moratorium on new data centers, beat Republican Gov. Greg Abbott—Wells Fargo estimates 27% of planned data center gigawatts are in Texas. Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia also campaigned on restricting data center development.

The opposition is not purely partisan. Abbott paused new data center permits in September pending a grid audit, and Hinojosa campaigned on extending that moratorium. Hinojosa likely won’t need a new law, since Abbott’s pause on grid connections already freezes data center permits.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5498. Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Oct 31, 2026 at 8:45 amOctober 31, 2026 at 8:47 am

#5496. Asia can’t afford a ‘cloudless’ day. That means paying attention to undersea cables

Kapil Kumar Jain is vice president of global network services at Tata Communications.

Picture a “cloudless” day—not in the meteorological sense, but one in which digital operations come to a sudden, catastrophic halt. Financial transactions stall. AI applications lose access to data. Supply chains slow, and customer experiences suffer.

It may sound improbable, yet recent events suggest otherwise. In 2024, subsea cable damage caused widespread internet outages that disrupted banks, fintech platforms and cloud-based businesses across Africa; in 2025, Red Sea cable cuts severely disrupted access across Asia and the Middle East. Internet traffic was rerouted through longer paths, increasing latency for cloud services and adding costs for businesses reliant on real-time digital operations.

These incidents are a reminder that what we call “the cloud” is neither virtual nor invincible. We often imagine it floating somewhere above us. In reality, it lies at the bottom of the ocean: More than 99% of all international data is carried not by satellites but by a physical backbone of subsea cables.

The regional digital economy runs uninterrupted only because companies made continuous, heavy investment in critical transit hubs like India and Singapore.

AI is placing unprecedented demands on the cloud, the foundation of today’s digital economy. AI workloads and hyperscale data centres need ever-greater bandwidth—with 400 gigabits (gbps) per second now the baseline and 800 gbps already emerging.

As countries and businesses race to scale AI, much of the focus has been on compute and data centres. But the networks connecting those systems need to keep pace as well. That raises a critical question for Asia: is the region overlooking a key AI infrastructure bottleneck?

Without sufficient investment in subsea cables and end-to-end networks, businesses could spend heavily on AI infrastructure only to see the returns eroded by disruption, higher operating costs and unreliable access to data.

For the C-suite, that presents a looming crisis: while AI investment is a board-level strategic priority for 77% of enterprise leaders, 65% of enterprises continue to operate on legacy or still-developing infrastructure, according to a Tata Communications study.

With AI workloads making global traffic patterns increasingly unpredictable, enterprises need dynamic, flexible data-centre-to-data-centre connectivity that can scale rapidly with demand to protect the bottom line and operational stability. Meeting this need will require continued investment from network providers in the infrastructure and capabilities needed to deliver scalable, resilient connectivity.

Most discussions of Singapore’s AI ambitions revolve around compute capacity, talent and regulation. Those are all important. But they overlook what happens when the data that AI systems depend on cannot be transmitted quickly, reliably or securely.

Singapore and India are emerging as two of the region’s most important data transit hubs, underpinned by their strategic locations and growing digital infrastructure. Singapore serves as a gateway to Southeast Asia, with one of the world’s densest concentrations of data centres. Meanwhile, India acts as a link between Asia, the Middle East and Europe, supported by major cable landing points and expanding data centre capacity in cities such as Mumbai and Chennai. Together, these strengths make both countries important hubs for international data traffic, underscoring the need for resilient and diverse connectivity routes to keep data moving efficiently between major financial centres and commercial workloads.

The industry needs to rethink how it approaches network architecture. For decades, infrastructure was built to support predictable, linear traffic. Today, infrastructure must now accommodate increasingly volatile AI-driven data demands.

This requires better integration  between subsea cables, terrestrial fibre and individual data centres, as a bottleneck at a coastal landing station can immediately negate the speed of a transoceanic cable.

However, keeping these cables secure and running requires far more than laying fiber in the ocean. True resilience demands a coordinated focus across four dimensions: capacity planning, network diversity, protection and repair readiness, and disciplined lifecycle operations.

This behind-the-scenes management—including robust monitoring, strategic spares management, tight integration of subsea and terrestrial networks, and clearly defined long-term governance—is what ensures a single cable cut does not become a regional blackout.

Crucially, this industry-led push is now being reinforced by public policy. The recent adoption of the Enhanced ASEAN Guidelines for Strengthening Resilience and Repair of Submarine Cables—which recommends capping repair processing times at 10 days—is a vital step forward. Regional policymakers are making rapid repair readiness of economic stability.

For businesses,  the practical consequence is a change in what gets funded. Compute and data centres often take priority in investment decisions because their capacity and returns are visible. Meanwhile, the cables, landing stations and alternative routes that keep them connected are less visible, and can be harder to justify as investments in their own right. Yet, the trade-off is clear: underinvestment in connectivity risks leaving expensive AI infrastructure vulnerable to disruption, congestion and higher operating costs. Connectivity must be treated as an essential and strategic asset not simply an operational cost hidden in the IT budget. The cloud begins beneath the ocean. As AI adoption accelerates, Singapore’s competitiveness as a global digital hub will depend on the strength of that invisible lifeline beneath the sea.
