#5495. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5494. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5493. Here’s What Makes the CEO of a $15 Billion Company Stop Reading a Document: ‘I Can Tell Pretty Quickly’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This leader has little patience for this kind of writing, tossing reports away as soon as he detects it.

Writing and editing are the most common uses of AI among U.S. workers. In Gallup’s May 2026 survey, 51% of workplace AI users said they used the technology for those purposes.

Now the CEO of $15 billion GoDaddy, the world’s largest domain name provider, is pushing back against those popular use cases. In a new interview with Business Insider, GoDaddy CEO Aman Bhutani said he won’t outsource his writing to AI, and he has little patience for employees who send him AI-written work.

“If somebody sends me a document and I can tell pretty quickly it was written by AI, I don’t read it,” Bhutani said in the interview. “Because if the person couldn’t take the time to write it, then I definitely shouldn’t take the time to read it.”

Bhutani said there is a difference between using AI for clarification and letting it completely take over the writing. Workers can turn to the technology to better understand an unfamiliar word or phrase, but they must be able to turn their own ideas into a clear narrative, he said.

Turning ideas into compelling narratives is a critical skill, Bhutani added. Employees who write documents on their own are continuously practicing “the art of iteration,” or refining their written work and improving over time.

“What I’m really looking for is: What was the original observation? What was the original hypothesis, and what got you interested in this idea? Why do you think it matters? Right?” he said. “Because AI only knows what the internet already knows. It doesn’t know what we know deep inside us, and there are ideas coming from us all the time.”

Bhutani looks for a few tells when reading someone’s work. He notes that many of his colleagues speak English as a second language, so he is suspicious if they submit unusually polished prose.

Length can also raise a red flag. Some pieces run too long, while others are short but written in a recognizable “punchy and clear” tone that marks AI.

Researchers at Florida State University have found that common words such as “delve,” “intricate,” “realm” and “underscore” can be signs that AI wrote a block of text, especially when these keywords appear repeatedly.

AI also has some common stylistic habits. For example, it offers repeated contrast formulas: “It’s not just X — it’s Y.” It also relies on flowery metaphors, such as describing a subject as an “intricate tapestry.”

AI additionally yields perfect grammar and a plethora of em dashes. It provides an overly uniform structure, with similarly sized sections, repeated lists and conclusions that restate the introduction. It also generates inflated language, with grand claims and elaborate wording.

However, those clues alone aren’t proof that AI wrote a piece of text. AI detection tools like Turnitin can misidentify human writing. Turnitin advises against using its results alone to take action against a writer.

#5492. Tech stocks are suffering their biggest selloff since Covid, as investors see premature end to AI datacenter boom

It may have been Blue Tsunami on Tuesday but it was a sea of red that washed over tech stocks on Thursday, covering everything from chips and datacenter companies to software and gig economy firms, as investors panicked that the U.S. midterm election results will bring the AI boom to a premature halt, or at least, a significant slowdown.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down more than 1,340 points, or 5.2% in midday trading, shedding more than $3 trillion in market cap, and representing its biggest daily drop since the Liberation Day tariff announcement in April 2025, according to Bloomberg data. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Sector index, which tracks the 30 largest companies in the chips business, was down more than 1,000 points—on track for its single biggest day loss since March 2020.

Some of the biggest names in tech took it on the chin, with Facebook parent company Meta down 3.4%, Microsoft down 2.8%, and Nvidia down 8%.

Thursday’s selloff dragged down the entire market, marking a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when shares rallied following the Democrats’ retaking of the Senate and House of Representatives in the midterm elections. Voters overwhelmingly approved candidates and ballot measures that sought to curtail the buildout of AI data centers in the U.S.

That reality seems to have hit tech stock investors more forcefully on Thursday, as some early signs of the changing business conditions came into focus.

Meta President Dina Powell McCormick, speaking at a conference organized by the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday, acknowledged the new hurdles. Building data centers in the U.S. is “going to be harder,” she said. “I can also tell you that every hyperscaler is now thinking about ‘Do we need to build outside the United States?’ Because they’re enormous investments, hedging those investments is a wise thing to do.”

Dan Ives, the usually bullish analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors Thursday that he now expects the tech industry’s capex growth to peak next year, instead of in 2028 or 2029.

That capex spree has been an engine of the U.S. economy over the past two years as companies such as Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle, as well as new so-called neocloud companies, raced to build data centers to run AI services. The companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars for the chips, computers, and networking gear, in addition to land, energy, and construction, to erect the data centers.

“While Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027 the growth rate into 2028 will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map especially in the state of Texas,” Ives wrote.

“We estimate on the low end 10% of the planned 800-1,000 AI focused data centers in the US will now be wiped off the roadmap, with potentially up to 20% of these facing a much longer regulatory road that could further impact the capacity buildout in the US over the next few years,” Ives wrote.

Chip stocks were some of the worst hit, with Micron, the one of the world’s top 3 makers of memory chips, down roughly 14% and AMD, a rival to Nvidia, also down 14%.

Simeon Wallis, chief investment officer at Aprio Wealth Management, told Fortune that uncertainty around data center expansion in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio is leading to worries about AI industry growth. “We see that uncertainty reflected disproportionately in semiconductors, an industry that has been a major beneficiary of AI infrastructure investment,” said Wallis, whose firm manages $6.1 billion in assets.

Neocloud companies, which have taken on large amounts of debt to build data centers that compete with the likes of Amazon and Google, were particularly hard hit as well. Coreweave, one of the leading neocloud companies, was down 9% on Thursday, and on track for an 18% decline over the past two days.

By contrast, Google, one of the industry’s largest cloud  providers, with a search advertising business powering its business, was down a more modest 1.6% on Thursday.

The turmoil triggered by data center worries spread across the broader tech sector throughout Thursday. Software stocks like Salesforce and Snowflake were down 3.6% and 6.4% respectively. Figma, a maker of design software which reported stronger than expected Q3 revenue on Wednesday, was down 17%.

Even gig economy and streaming media companies like DoorDash, Uber, Spotify, and Netflix were all down by multiple percentage points by the time the market closed Thursday.

“Ultimately, we believe that markets can over-react in the short term to speculating who future winners and losers are,” said Wallis, of Aprio Wealth Management.

With additional reporting by Scott DeCarlo and Catherina Gioino.

Alexei Oreskovic is the Tech editor at Fortune.

#5491. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5490. What College Admissions Can Teach Entrepreneurs About the Art of Not Selling

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

What do college applicants desperate to impress admissions officers have in common with entrepreneurs desperate to win clients? Both make the same mistake. They oversell.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every year at Ivy Coach, our college admissions counseling firm, we encounter a subset of students who come to us for PostMortems after being rejected by their dream colleges, having succumbed to the irresistible urge to turn their Personal Statement into a sales pitch.

They’ve earned straight A’s, founded clubs, conducted research and won competitions. And they can’t resist cramming every last achievement into their Personal Statement, as though an exhaustive list of accomplishments will convince an admissions officer to admit them.

We practically have to hit them over the head. Stop selling! That’s what they’re doing, of course. They’re begging an admissions officer: Admit me! Admit me! Look at everything I’ve accomplished! And you know what? It makes them profoundly unlikable. The same mistake is made every day by entrepreneurs who can’t resist selling themselves.

At Ivy Coach, we teach students that the best college admissions essays don’t recount achievements. Awards, honors and accomplishments should never be fodder for an admissions essay. After all, the application’s activities section already serves that purpose. Instead, the most compelling essays tell one small story. Rather than recounting how a student overcame adversity to become student body president or came from behind to win a conference championship, that story should reveal how they hope to shape the world in a singular, often small way.

We call that singular quality a student’s “hook.” And when an admissions officer finishes reading an application, they should feel they’ve met someone who will contribute to their campus community through that distinctive lens. The key isn’t to say more, but instead to make what you do say count. Sometimes the most persuasive thing you can do is resist the urge to keep talking.

The same holds true for entrepreneurs speaking with prospective clients. You don’t need to overwhelm people with reasons to choose you. Sometimes, knowing when to stop selling, and when to simply be quiet, is what inspires the greatest confidence.

One of the easiest traps for entrepreneurs to fall into is overselling when the conversation turns to fees. At Ivy Coach, prospective clients sometimes ask why we charge what we charge. But that doesn’t warrant a defensive explanation of overhead, the unique expertise our consultants lend, or the cost of running a business. Our fees are our fees. As I once told The New York Times, “Who can say what is too much in America? If someone wants to pay a fee that you command, they have that right.” Who knew stating something so obvious would earn me the paper’s Quote of the Day?

With a track record spanning three-and-a-half decades, an established reputation and generations of families who value Ivy Coach’s work, there’s no need to justify our fees any more than a student needs to justify their worthiness of admission by reciting every one of their accomplishments.

When someone asks you to justify your fees, resist the temptation to deliver a lengthy sales pitch. You don’t need to convince everyone that your services are worth their price. Some people will see the value, while others won’t. That’s business. And chances are, the people who insist you defend your fees aren’t the clients you want in the first place.

Another occasion when entrepreneurs fall into the trap of overselling is when a prospective client announces they’re interviewing several competing firms. Wonderful, that’s their prerogative. Frankly, it’s a little rude to announce it since nobody needs a running commentary on a prospective client’s shopping expedition. Just do your homework. But too many entrepreneurs respond by getting defensive, explaining why their competitors aren’t as good, offering discounts and rattling off credentials. Before long, they’re practically begging for the business.

Sound familiar? It’s the college applicant stuffing every accomplishment into a Personal Statement. Choose me! Choose me! At Ivy Coach, we’re not interested in playing that game. Our track record speaks for itself.

The entrepreneurs who inspire the greatest confidence are those who understand what makes their businesses different and don’t feel compelled to prove their worth at every opportunity. The same is true of college applicants. You don’t become memorable by telling someone how extraordinary you are. Instead, you become memorable by allowing them to discover it for themselves.

And therein lies the paradox of persuasion. The harder you try to sell yourself, the less appealing you become. So stop reciting your accomplishments. Stop defending your prices. Stop worrying about competitors. Tell your story, stand behind your work, and let people decide for themselves. After all, nobody likes being sold to. Whether you’re trying to win a client or earn a college acceptance, the moment you start begging to be chosen is the moment you make yourself easier to reject.

Every year at Ivy Coach, our college admissions counseling firm, we encounter a subset of students who come to us for PostMortems after being rejected by their dream colleges, having succumbed to the irresistible urge to turn their Personal Statement into a sales pitch.

They’ve earned straight A’s, founded clubs, conducted research and won competitions. And they can’t resist cramming every last achievement into their Personal Statement, as though an exhaustive list of accomplishments will convince an admissions officer to admit them.

We practically have to hit them over the head. Stop selling! That’s what they’re doing, of course. They’re begging an admissions officer: Admit me! Admit me! Look at everything I’ve accomplished! And you know what? It makes them profoundly unlikable. The same mistake is made every day by entrepreneurs who can’t resist selling themselves.

#5489. The Iran war has cost U.S. households nearly $2,000 each. New strikes could keep the bill climbing

On Oct. 8, President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that “we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.” On Nov. 2, the day before Americans voted, U.S. forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island.

U.S. officials told CNN the Qeshm attack was a defensive response to Iranian forces using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets. In a Fox News interview that aired that night, Trump suggested there had been no recent fighting.

The Qeshm attack was not an isolated event. Officials told ABC News that limited “defensive strikes” had been carried out in recent weeks and not publicized to avoid signaling a return to major combat operations.

The strikes are small next to earlier phases of the war. But they come at a fragile moment for energy markets, which had just priced in hopes of a diplomatic exit, and as the U.S. heads into heating season.

Gilbert Metcalf, a visiting professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former deputy assistant secretary for environment and energy at the U.S. Treasury Department, says the strikes raise the odds of the outcome markets fear most.

“The risk to global oil markets and, by extension, the global economy as we head into winter is the potential for Iranian strikes against shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or against oil and gas infrastructure in the region,” Metcalf tells Fortune. “Continued strikes against Iran, albeit so-called ‘defensive strikes,’ only increase the likelihood of their undertaking those attacks.”

Even restraint from Tehran may not help much. “Even if the Iranians hold back, any increased military activity in the region heightens the risk of retaliation, which adversely affects markets,” he says. “Oil prices will remain persistently high in the face of these risks, and this is particularly concerning as we move into winter and the need for oil and gas for home heating.”

U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran that began Feb. 28 set off a regional war, according to the Congressional Research Service. Iran has retaliated against targets across the Middle East, including a pumping station on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, and has used attacks on commercial shipping to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.

The two sides agreed to a ceasefire in April and signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17. The agreement collapsed within weeks amid renewed fighting and formally expired in August. By September, the CRS described the conflict as a war of attrition.

The price tag keeps rising. The U.S. military has spent more than $47 billion on the war, Reuters reported on Oct. 27, citing Pentagon data. That is up from the $37.5 billion Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth estimated in July, and more than $29 billion of it goes to replacing expended munitions.

Households are paying, too. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimates the war has cost the average U.S. household nearly $2,000, CNN reported. About $1,100 of that comes from higher energy and transportation costs, with higher interest rates and a share of military spending making up the rest.

“Nationwide, that adds up to $265 billion,” Zandi wrote on X on Oct. 12.

Much of the pain runs through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about 20 million barrels of oil a day before the war. Qeshm Island, about 14 miles from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas, is central to Iran’s ability to control traffic through it, and Iran has stepped up attacks on commercial ships transiting the strait in recent weeks, according to ABC News.

There is no easy workaround. Metcalf told Fortune last month that even Saudi Arabia’s plan to send 10 million barrels of oil a day around Hormuz may barely move prices.

Energy costs hung over the campaign. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate on Nov. 3, and Vice President JD Vance put it bluntly: “The reason we lost is the war.”

Oil reacted quickly. Brent crude fell more than 9% on Nov. 4 as traders bet the results would push the White House toward a deal, CNBC reported, and Trump said he had no immediate plans to strike Iran.

Iran has long been expected to wait out the vote. In September, Fortune’s Jordan Blum reported that Tehran was unlikely to let the war end until after the midterms. Mediators were awaiting U.S. and Iranian responses to their latest proposal as of Nov. 2, CNN reported.

Metcalf isn’t convinced the relief will last. “The blue wave sparked hopes that the Iran war might be resolved diplomatically and, not surprisingly, oil prices fell sharply,” he says. “That optimism may be short-sighted if Trump decides that, with the election behind him, he can increase military pressure on Iran.”

#5488. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5487. Flattening Your Organization Comes With Real Risks. Here’s What Companies Often Overlook.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Fewer management layers can mean faster decisions, but what happens to the work those managers were doing?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you’ve ever waited days for approval on something seemingly straightforward, it’s easy to see the attraction of a flatter organization: fewer handoffs, faster decisions and more autonomy.

There’s a deeper question, though. Before removing a management layer, it is important to have an understanding of what the people in that layer do — and who will take on those tasks in their absence.

There are real repercussions that need to be considered before a management layer is removed. Managers have both tangible tasks and responsibilities, as well as the less tangible ones that go along with leadership. Both of these need to be taken into account when considering a flatter organizational structure.

Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace reports that manager engagement worldwide declined by about 29% between 2022 and 2025. That’s a huge drop in the percentage of managers who feel involved in and enthusiastic about their jobs — and it is an indicator that something is amiss.

While the research doesn’t tell us that flattening management caused this decline, it prompts us to look beyond how many people report to a manager and ask more subtle questions. Under the new structure, what do people need in terms of leadership? And will their manager have the time and skills to devote to it?

An analysis from Boston University’s Questrom School of Business explains what’s at stake. Middle managers act as connectors between senior leaders’ strategy and the people carrying it out — putting them under pressure from both sides. Leaders above them expect results, while employees need direction and support to deliver those results.

Coaches on my team see this frequently. When management layers disappear, those remaining get squeezed even more. Thinning those roles can weaken coordination, learning and the development of future leaders. Here are a few examples:

Senior leaders move up a launch date, expecting a flatter structure to help everyone move faster. But the manager responsible has the same team and existing customer commitments to meet. They’re accountable for the earlier deadline without any more capacity to deliver it. They’re caught between pushing their team harder and pushing back on the expectations above them.

A strong technical performer is promoted into a bigger leadership role because the company needs someone capable to take it on. But they’re still learning how to delegate, handle conflict and make decisions when there’s no clear answer. They’re accountable for a broader range of work before they’ve had enough practice leading at a new level. Under pressure, they may fall back on what they know best: solving problems themselves, even as the role requires them to help others do it.

A team uses AI to produce several proposals in the time it once took to develop one. Senior leaders see faster output and expect faster decisions. But the manager still has to check the assumptions, weigh the risks and decide which ones are worth pursuing. More work reaches their desk without more time to review it. They’re caught between keeping up with the new pace and giving each decision the human attention and discernment it deserves.

I’m not suggesting the answer is to keep every management layer. It’s making sure the new structure gives the remaining managers what they need to be successful: clear authority to make decisions, agreed-upon priorities and the number of direct reports they can realistically support. They need time to lead — helping their teams learn and improve — rather than spending every day simply putting out the most urgent fires.

If AI handles more entry-level work and companies keep removing management layers, where will emerging leaders get the experience that prepares them to lead?

Leadership development can’t wait until someone gets the title. Companies need to create those opportunities deliberately. Here are five techniques you can use to develop leadership skills:

People learn by watching experienced managers work through disagreements, explain decisions and handle uncertainty. Invite an emerging leader into a planning conversation, then talk through why you made a particular tradeoff. Let them hear the reasoning they wouldn’t get from the meeting summary.

Give people opportunities to lead a project, coach a colleague or coordinate work across teams before they’re responsible for an entire team. Be clear about what decisions they own, and make sure someone is available to help them work through questions.

AI can generate options quickly, but human judgment is still vital. When someone brings a recommendation, ask what they checked, what they ruled out and why. Help them develop confidence in their reasoning, including recognizing when they need another perspective.

Knowing how to give feedback isn’t the same as sitting across from someone who’s upset by what you’ve said. Emerging leaders need repeated opportunities to practice feedback, delegation and difficult conversations in the messiness of real situations with other humans — with guidance afterward.

Fewer titles shouldn’t mean fewer ways to grow. Give people progressively broader assignments and look at how they handle them. That gives the company evidence of who’s ready for more responsibility, even without a promotion at every step.

Having fewer managers may make the org chart look more efficient, but it doesn’t make the day-to-day work of leadership disappear. A flatter organization can work when executive leadership rethinks the workload, authority and support that go along with organizational flattening.

Otherwise, they’re merely leaving fewer managers to carry a bigger load, which can lead to faster burnout and turnover. The challenge is to give managers what they need to lead well today — and prepare a new generation of leaders for the future.

If you’ve ever waited days for approval on something seemingly straightforward, it’s easy to see the attraction of a flatter organization: fewer handoffs, faster decisions and more autonomy.

There’s a deeper question, though. Before removing a management layer, it is important to have an understanding of what the people in that layer do — and who will take on those tasks in their absence.

There are real repercussions that need to be considered before a management layer is removed. Managers have both tangible tasks and responsibilities, as well as the less tangible ones that go along with leadership. Both of these need to be taken into account when considering a flatter organizational structure.

#5486. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5485. 60% of Workers Have a “Work Enemy.” Here’s the Strange Trick That Disarms Them

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Make them your Newman. You’ll be happier for it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Feeling stuck in a situation? Trying to resolve a difficult challenge?

Here’s a strange solution, but I promise it works: Just pretend that you’re in a sitcom.

Framing your situation as a sitcom allows you to view yourself as the protagonist of your own story. It encourages you to channel the confidence and self-assuredness of iconic movie characters like Ferris Bueller or Elle Woods. This perspective also infuses appreciation into almost any circumstance by transforming the dull, bland backdrop of your daily life into a well-thought-out set with interesting characters and details that you’ll want to pay attention to.

Consider it: Shows like The Office didn’t become so popular because the characters all got along swimmingly. The fun of watching The Office comes from seeing people with very different personalities and goals get along and observing how their peccadilloes create conflict in real time.

Rather than treating those around you as people you need to tolerate, the sitcom perspective can help you see them as personalities and personas that are more endearing and easier to understand.

Take the character Newman in Seinfeld. Newman is the archnemesis of Jerry, the main character of the show. It is impossible for Jerry and Newman not to interact, because they live in the same building and share a best friend, Kramer, who is also Jerry’s next-door neighbor. Jerry and Newman are diametrically opposed about everything, except the New York Mets, and often refer to each other as the “sworn enemy” or just “pure evil.” “Hello, Newman” has become one of the most iconic lines in TV history because of the somewhat sinister way Jerry greets Newman every time they cross paths.

We all have our Newmans in life, especially at work. According to a 2019 survey of over 7,000 employees by the United Kingdom’s largest job listing platform, Totaljobs, 60 percent of workers have a “work enemy.” In fact, almost 50 percent of those polled had at least one, 43 percent had more than one, and almost 10 percent said they saw most of their colleagues as enemies.

At my core, I want to figure out how to decrease these numbers, so let’s talk about how seeing a situation through the lens of a sitcom can help us feel less stuck at work.

Let’s say my work enemy is Barbara. I see Barbara as a work enemy for these reasons:

But when I see Barbara as the “sitcom frenemy,” she now feels more approachable:

Over the years, I collected a perspective like this for just about everyone I interacted with, from my friendliest coworkers to my archnemeses. It helped me feel as though I had control over the dynamic of the relationship, as well as my own mood. It reassured me to know that I could turn down the dial of any unpleasant interaction or tense conversation as I saw fit.

I may not have been able to choose what was happening to me directly, but I could choose how to frame it. By seeing myself as the main character of a bizarre sitcom, I dictated how I used my energy instead of letting work drama decide for me.

Want more ways to feel better, and appreciate everything around you? This essay was excerpted from Timm Chiusano’s new book, How to Get Addicted to Appreciation.

Feeling stuck in a situation? Trying to resolve a difficult challenge?

Here’s a strange solution, but I promise it works: Just pretend that you’re in a sitcom.

Framing your situation as a sitcom allows you to view yourself as the protagonist of your own story. It encourages you to channel the confidence and self-assuredness of iconic movie characters like Ferris Bueller or Elle Woods. This perspective also infuses appreciation into almost any circumstance by transforming the dull, bland backdrop of your daily life into a well-thought-out set with interesting characters and details that you’ll want to pay attention to.

#5484. Cloudflare’s appeal won’t fix what’s broken in Delaware’s Chancery Court

The morning after we wrote in Fortune about a controversial Chancery Court decision involving Cloudflare, Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster moved with uncommon speed to certify an interlocutory appeal of his ruling to the Delaware Supreme Court.

Corporate boards might read that as a sign the system is correcting itself. They shouldn’t, at least not yet.

The appeal was necessary because Laster used an unusually expansive reading of “good faith” to enjoin the Cloudflare board’s decision about its capital structure.

With corporate anchoring fees rivaling personal income taxes as Delaware’s primary source of revenue, Delaware’s wise leaders, including its governor and its legislature, saw this exodus coming, and tried to stem its root cause. In March 2025, Delaware passed Senate Bill 21 (SB 21), the most significant rewrite of its corporate code in a generation, to stop the flow of companies out of the state. SB 21 was generally recognized to have been a direct response to a run of activist rulings from the Court of Chancery, which were widely seen as blatant judicial overreach.

The spirit of SB 21 is simple: if a board routes a possibly “conflicted” deal through a committee of independent directors with real power to reject it, the deal is considered “kosher.” This means no injunctions, no damages, no trial.

Indeed, Laster’s 142-page opinion concedes the legitimacy of SB 21 and its applicability to this case. He held the directors were independent. He held they were not negligent. He wrote that their process showed “all the outward signs of diligent and careful effort.” By his own account, virtually every requirement the legislature wrote was met by the Cloudflare board.

He enjoined the transaction anyway, on a novel basis. SB 21 does require that the committee act “in good faith,” but Laster’s route was to re-define what good faith entails – even though the legislative intent of SB 21 and the surrounding debate in the legislature, clearly shows that the Delaware legislature intended SB 21 to be more deferential to independent boards, not less.

The term “good faith” was not a third level of diligence beyond the duty of care and duty of loyalty, but merely presumed to be the spirit of board actions. Before this, good faith had been previously generally assumed, in deference to independent boards, with nary any heightened review threshold, much less any invocation to enjoin a transaction.

Instead, he pointed in part to the fact that the board used Signal to communicate about sensitive strategic information they presumably did not want competitors obtaining, irrespective of litigation, and to a CEO who was known to have a hot temper, even though the temperament of the entrepreneur is irrelevant to good faith and typical of creative businesses in technology, media, fashion and the like.

From those disconnected scraps, the court inferred that the committee was serving the founders rather than bargaining against them, or what Laster, borrowing from the 2011 Southern Peru case, called “a controlled mindset”, as proof of possible lack of good faith by the committee.

In analyzing Laster’s novel interpretation of what “good faith” means, readers might ask whether Laster was merely applying the statute, SB 21, rather than inventing a new standard. But that flies in the face of the legislative history of SB 21, which clearly suggests the intent of the Delaware legislature was to try to drive greater predictability and greater deference to independent boards, rather than drive more elevated scrutiny of those same boards. Against that backdrop, Laster’s idiosyncratic, broader reading of ‘good faith’ substantively guts the protections SB21 was meant to provide.

But even more importantly, and legally salient; Laster’s interpretation of ‘good faith’ is far from what “good faith” has always historically meant in Delaware, from a legal perspective. The existing Delaware definition of bad faith is grounded in scienter, the requirement of showing that individuals acted with knowledge and intent of wrongdoing, together with the requirement that each board member be assessed individually to determine whether a majority intentionally acted in bad faith. That is the Disney line of cases.

In 2006, the Delaware Supreme Court defined bad faith as “intentional dereliction of duty, a conscious disregard for one’s responsibilities,” and held that gross negligence, “without more, cannot constitute bad faith.” Stone v. Ritter that same year made good faith a “subsidiary element” of the duty of loyalty rather than a freestanding duty. And Lyondell in 2009 held that directors who merely “failed to do all that they should have” breached only their duty of care, while “only if they knowingly and completely failed to undertake their responsibilities” could they be found disloyal.

Startlingly, Laster largely set aside that definition in practice. A board’s understandable use of Signal to communicate about sensitive strategic information, or a CEO known to have a hot temper, amounts to nothing even remotely resembling scienter, which is knowing or willful misconduct. The opinion likewise faults the committee for not obtaining a fairness opinion while conceding, in its own footnote, that “Delaware courts have stated that there is no duty to obtain a fairness opinion.” Under Lyondell, a process that could have been better is a question of care, not loyalty, and Laster found no failure of care.

Most tellingly, he acknowledged that without what he called the defendants’ “credibility problems,” he “could have concluded” the safe harbor applied. In other words, the statute’s protection now turns on whether a trial judge likes the witnesses.

If a board can be independent, informed, and diligent and still be found to have acted in bad faith, directors are left without a clear rule to follow. That uncertainty is exactly what is pushing companies to reincorporate elsewhere.

A disputed record, headed to the Supreme Court

Laster’s certification also characterizes the facts in ways we believe are wrong, and it is the trial court’s account of the record that the Supreme Court will review.

He wrote that “the Committee looked for and found an academic who would say that…maintaining founder control would be good for the Company.” Our research, published for years in academic outlets and in Fortune, describes when dual-class shares fail as well as when they work. We have found that well-governed, founder-led companies with dual-class shares have, as a group, outperformed, and that such structures should expire when they no longer make sense or are abused. Laster also suggested that the company’s financial advisors had data disputing our conclusions. However, in reality, the financial advisors did not, have any such counter evidence,  as their own presentations make clear.

He also ruled on the credibility of parties he never met, relying on a one-hour hearing on the paper record alone. The Supreme Court therefore has no firsthand insight from the trial judge to which it could defer.

The Delaware Supreme Court has reversed Laster in more than 30 decisions, but it has repeatedly remanded those cases back to his courtroom. For example, the Boardwalk Pipeline litigation, stemming from Loews’ 2018 buyout of Boardwalk’s public unitholders, has bounced between the two courts for eight years and remains unresolved. Litigation on that scale is a costly distraction for management and boards, on top of fees that can run from $60 million to more than half a billion dollars per company.

For example, when the Delaware Supreme Court reversed him in his controversial Aruba decision in 2019, they issued a rare rebuke with withering criticism, noting that Laster’s opinion “could be seen” as “a results-oriented move to generate an odd result compelled by his personal frustration at being reversed in Dell,” that the approach “was in no way dictated by a rational reading of Dell,” that his agency-cost reasoning was “not grounded in the record,” and that by injecting a valuation theory the plaintiff “had not itself posited,” he “injected due process and fairness problems into the proceedings.”

While that sounds like a promising development, the court had the power to reassign remanded cases to a different judge, and has not done so. This undermines their own reversal of the Chancery Court, repeatedly throwing the firm back into the arms of its previous judge to invent a serious of unique reasons to derail the deal.

Certifying an appeal is not the same as a predictable legal regime, and predictability is what boards cite when they leave Delaware. Until the Supreme Court clarifies what “good faith” requires of an independent, diligent board in a predictable and non-arbitrary way, and until appellate reversals carry real consequences on remand, directors should assume that a sound process may not be enough to protect their decisions in Chancery.

As the Roman poet Juvenal asked, “Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?” Who guards the guards?

Disclosure: Cloudflare’s special committee retained us, given our widely recognize expertise as governance scholars, to present our published research on when dual-class share structures help and hurt companies, as it deliberated its own structure based upon our analysis of the total universe of major firms with such arrangements. We were not asked to opine on the terms of Cloudflare’s proposed reclassification, did not do so, and take no position on its design. We have no relationship with Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is the Lester Crown Professor in Management Practice and Senior Associate Dean at Yale School of Management.

Steven Tian is the director of research at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.

#5483. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5482. Buyers Stopped Believing Pitches. Give Them Something They Can Verify.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Software now writes the pitch, sends it and even personalizes it, so buyers have learned to discount all of it. Here’s what works now.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Anyone can write a good pitch now. A decent cold email, a tidy case study, a landing page full of confident claims. It takes a tool and about 10 minutes. Software now sends the outreach too, in volumes no person could match. Even the personal touches are written by it.

Buyers know all of this, and they have adjusted. The businesses winning new customers right now stopped asking to be believed and started letting people check.

Think about what a pitch actually is. It is the seller describing their own work in the best possible light. That was always a little suspect. Now it is also free to produce at scale, which means every competitor sounds equally polished and equally sure of themselves.

Buyers have noticed. The TrustRadius 2026 B2B Buying Disconnect report surveyed 1,862 technology buyers in January 2026. Among the buyers who used AI during their purchase, 94% fact-checked its answers at least some of the time. They are not only doubting vendors anymore. They are doubting the tools they use to research vendors.

The same report found that 74% of buyers use reviews to inform their decisions, and 83% shortlisted three or fewer products. Put those together. Buyers check outside sources, then narrow the field fast. If your claims can’t survive that check, you are out before the first conversation. The survey covers technology buyers, but the habit will sound familiar to anyone who sells anything.

The obvious fix is personalization. Mention the buyer’s recent post or their funding round or their new job. For a while, that worked, because it showed someone had paid attention.

It doesn’t show that anymore. When software writes the first line too, a personal detail only proves the sender has a decent data source. Most of us have received enough of these to spot the pattern, and a pattern with your name filled in is still a pattern.

A Gartner survey of about 645 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2025, found that 67% prefer a buying experience without a sales rep. A second release from the same survey found that 69% prefer to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep.

Those sound opposed, but they say one thing. Buyers want to evaluate on their own first, then talk to a person who will stand behind the answer. A cold email that asks for 15 minutes gives them neither.

Here is the version I would use. It rests on one idea. When words are cheap, the only signal left is effort the buyer can see.

Lead with something they can judge in under a minute. Skip the request for a meeting. Send a marked-up version of their landing page, a one-page teardown of their pricing or a short sample made from their own material. They should be able to evaluate it without replying, booking or talking to anyone.

Software can fake this, too. Marketer Dennis Yu described getting a seven-page AI-written audit in a cold email, with no real headlines or screenshots and a case study he says was made up. He saw through it. So give the buyer a way to tell. Real work names something only someone who looked would know. It includes one concrete fix. The buyer can check it in a minute. A named person will answer questions about it.

Send fewer. When tools make volume free, volume stops meaning anything. I would rather reach 20 prospects I studied than 2,000 I scraped. And put a person behind the follow-up. Reply fast and in your own words. Answer the hard question directly.

That advice is for cold outreach. Once you have paying customers, the free version runs into a different problem, and I learned it the hard way.

In my business, new clients could get one edited video before paying anything. When we started, 91.5% of trials turned into clients. We had fewer leads then and more time to focus on each one. Over the years, we added real clients, and their work came first. Trial edits got harder to fit in, and conversion dropped to 67%.

So we started charging a small fee for a single video. We also put a short fit call in front of it. Conversion from paid trial to customer is back to around 87%.

My read is that free work doesn’t scale because it competes with paid work for the same people’s time. A small fee pays for that time, so the trial gets the same attention as everything else. It also signals that the buyer is serious. They still judge real work before they commit, which was the point all along.

You don’t need a video for this. A small paid audit or a one-page plan works the same way. Keep it small enough that you can afford to do it often. And set the next step before you send anything, whether that is a call, a quote or a start date. A sample with no next step is a favor and not a sales process.

Anyone can write a good pitch now. A decent cold email, a tidy case study, a landing page full of confident claims. It takes a tool and about 10 minutes. Software now sends the outreach too, in volumes no person could match. Even the personal touches are written by it.

Buyers know all of this, and they have adjusted. The businesses winning new customers right now stopped asking to be believed and started letting people check.

Think about what a pitch actually is. It is the seller describing their own work in the best possible light. That was always a little suspect. Now it is also free to produce at scale, which means every competitor sounds equally polished and equally sure of themselves.

#5481. The AI boom is the first platform shift where there are ‘real advantages’ of building from Asia, says Antler’s founder and CEO Magnus Grimeland

Despite its fragmented markets and myriad of cultures and spoken languages, Asia is becoming an increasingly popular home for budding tech and AI entrepreneurs, according to Magnus Grimeland, the founder and CEO of venture capital firm Antler.

“Going to the U.S. to build companies is still very popular and we see that happening at scale,” Grimeland said at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Vietnam on Nov. 3. “[But] for the first time ever in one of these platform shifts, there are real advantages in Asia that will lead to a lot of the leading companies being built out of here.”

According to Crunchbase data, investors poured $42.8 billion into startup funding rounds across all of Asia in the second quarter of 2026—the highest quarterly total in over three years. In Grimeland’s telling, several factors make Asia an appealing home for startups: a rapidly growing electricity grid, and an abundance of advanced chips and AI engineering talent.

“If you look at global power production, there’s four times more power being generated and built in Asia per year than in Europe and the U.S. combined,” he explained. “Most of that is in China, but [it’s happening] in the rest of Asia as well… the cost of power has gone down drastically compared to what you can access in the U.S..”

Asia, too, is leading in the physical AI realm. “All the leading companies in that space are here,” Grimeland said. “There’s very, very few autonomous vehicles on the streets in the U.S…. [but there’s] one company in China that has more autonomous vehicles on the streets than the rest of the world combined.”

Yet, the allocation of venture funding remains hugely uneven within Asia. Thus far in 2026, 68.1%—or $96.1 billion of $141 billion—of VC funds entering Asia flowed into China, mainly to AI startups such as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and StepFun, according to Dealroom data. By contrast, only $10.7 billion of venture funding went to Southeast Asia during the first nine months of the year.

“I get this question all the time: “What kinds of AI deals are you seeing in the Philippines?”” said Franco Varona, managing partner at Foxmont Capital Partners, a Philippines-based early growth fund. “[But] we don’t have the infrastructure for an LLM developer. We don’t even have the infrastructure for AI apps to be developed in the Philippines.”

Varona, a Canada-born Filipino, argued that this environment creates different investment opportunities. “In developed markets, you can already benefit from the infrastructure which has been developed, and you can invest in innovators, because those innovators have everything around them that can help them out,” Varona said. “[But] when we think about investing in an emerging market like the Philippines, we think about it as investing in the infrastructure itself.”

To date, Foxmont has launched several themed funds, including one on digitization in the Philippines, and another focused on accessibility and affordability for Filipino consumers.

The unique corporate dynamic in Asia has also pushed the region’s long-running venture firms to launch new funding models. Singapore-headquartered VC firm Granite Asia’s private credit fund Libra Hybrid, for example, combines the characteristics of both debt and equity into a single financial instrument.

“A lot of businesses [in Asia] are family owned or part of conglomerates,” said Ming Eng, Granite Asia’s managing partner. “They may not be interested in dilution or going for an IPO at any point in time… but they still need strategic capital to help them grow, and that’s where we see a lot of opportunities to help founders and companies, [by] having a different form of capital other than [pure] equity.”

All three panelists remained bullish on Asia’s VC scene, despite recent geopolitical headwinds. “We are going into a world now where the balance of innovation is clearly shifting,” concluded Grimeland of Antler. “There’s a real chance that more than the majority of the most exciting and innovative companies in [the AI] space will have been built out of Asia, and that has never happened before.”

Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.
